Sender Name
` | | **No emojis** | Every card icon as inline SVG (``) in `.card-icon { background: rgba(201,169,63,0.12); }` | | **No "existing" framing** | Scrub: "existing / extends / reuses / ported / re-skin / on the platform" → purpose-built voice | | **No recipient-team-member names** | Generic recipient label only ("ModAE", "Client Representative") | | **No "proposal" wording** | Doc-type words throughout: "Project Plan", "Plan Code", "Effective Date", "will deliver" (not "proposes") | | **No enumerated out-of-scope** | One generic clause: "Material additions outside the six workstreams follow a written change-request process." | ### Stage 6 — Pre-render verification grep ```bash F="OUTPUT.html" echo "=== LOGOS ==="; grep -c '___ProjectPlan_.{html,pdf}` Example: `Betser_ModAE_WinTrack_WorkflowPlatform_ProjectPlan_BSL-2026-MODAE-WT01.html` Doc-code prefix matches the **sender's** entity prefix (e.g. `BSL-` for Betser Life), never the style-owner's prefix. ## Example Domains | Domain | Sender | Style owner | Source spec | Doc type | |--------|--------|-------------|-------------|----------| | IT consulting group | Indian subsidiary | Dubai parent | Client's workflow handover docx | Project Plan | | White-label SaaS reseller | Reseller LLP | Original product company | Client's tender RFP | Project Plan | | Architecture studio | Specialist studio | Multi-discipline parent | Client's brief | Design Plan | | Marketing agency | Account-led brand | Holding agency | Client's strategy ask | Engagement Plan | | Healthcare IT vendor | Local entity | Group HQ | Hospital's RFP | Implementation Plan | | Pharma services | Indian CRO | US parent | Sponsor's protocol | Project Plan | | Cybersecurity consultancy | Regional partner | Global brand | Customer's risk register | Engagement Plan | ## Anti-patterns - **Skipping Stage 1** (anchor identification) and starting to draft. Guarantees you copy a Proposal template into a Project Plan slot — 30 wording mistakes follow. - **Editing CSS from scratch** instead of cloning the canonical JotFlow analog. skills.name: Credential Survivorship Audit
skills.description: When a credentials-based failure recurs after a previous fix, the credential was only partially removed. Grep all config locations first, fix second, grep-verify after — before restarting the service. Also: test the underlying component directly (bypassing proxies) to isolate failure faster.
skills.body:
# Credential Survivorship Audit

## Problem

You fix an auth failure (expired key, quota-exceeded token, wrong credential) by removing the credential. The bot/service works again. A week or month later, the exact same failure message reappears. You go back and find the **same credential still present in a different location** you missed the first time.

Config-driven services (LLM gateways, OpenClaw, LangChain, etc.) store credentials in 3–10 places: config file env sections, per-agent auth profiles, OAuth state files, systemd/launchd service definitions, PM2 env, `.env` files, credential stores. A partial cleanup causes identical recurrence.

## The Recurrence Anti-Pattern

```
First incident → fix A → service restored
Second incident → same error message → same root cause, different location of credential
Third incident → ...
```

If the error message is identical to a prior incident, it almost always means the fix was incomplete — not that a new credential appeared.

## Solution

**Grep-before-fix, grep-verify-after.** Don't rely on memory of what you fixed last time.

### Step 1 — Grep all possible locations first

```bash
# Find EVERY occurrence of the credential name across the entire config dir
grep -r "ANTHROPIC\|anthropic" ~/.openclaw/
grep -r "OLD_API_KEY\|old_service" ~/.myapp/

# Or for a broader service root
grep -rn "CREDENTIAL_NAME" /root/.service-name/ /etc/service-name/ ~/.service-name/
```

This shows you ALL locations at once before you touch anything.

### Step 2 — Fix all locations in one pass

Don't fix one and restart. Fix every location you found in step 1:

```
config.json env section          → remove the key
per-agent/auth-profiles.json    → set to {"version":1,"profiles":{}}
per-agent/auth-state.json       → clear usageStats
credentials/oauth.json          → set to {}
systemd service file            → remove Environment=CREDENTIAL_*
launchd plist                   → remove EnvironmentVariables entries
PM2 ecosystem.config.js         → remove from env block
.env file                       → remove the line
```

### Step 3 — Grep-verify before restart

```bash
# Must return zero results
grep -r "CREDENTIAL_NAME" ~/.service-config/
# If anything comes back — fix it now, before restarting
```

### Step 4 — Test the underlying component directly

Before restarting the proxy/gateway layer, test the internal component directly to confirm the fix works:

```bash
# Bad: restart proxy, send a real user message, wait, check logs
pm2 restart my-proxy && ...

# Good: invoke the underlying command directly, see the output immediately
my-service run --agent my-agent --local -m "test" --timeout 20
```

Direct testing:
- Bypasses the proxy → failures are isolated to the service, not the proxy
- Returns output synchronously → no log-tailing needed
- Confirms the fix before any user traffic hits it
- Catches config validation errors (e.g., unrecognized keys) that only surface at runtime

Only restart the proxy **after** the direct test passes.

## Config Validation Trap

When editing a config file, only set keys that the service recognizes. An unrecognized key (even a sensible-looking one like `"model"`) silently or loudly breaks the config:

```bash
# Always validate config before restart
my-service doctor
my-service config validate
# Or just run the service in dry-run / --help mode to catch schema errors early
```

If the service has no validator, do a direct component test (step 4 above) — it will fail fast with a config error rather than silently misbehaving.

## Quick Reference Checklist

- [ ] `grep -r CREDENTIAL_NAME ~/.<service>/` → find all locations
- [ ] Remove credential from every location found
- [ ] `grep -r CREDENTIAL_NAME ~/.<service>/` → verify zero results
- [ ] Direct component test (bypass proxy) → confirm response
- [ ] Restart proxy/service
- [ ] Monitor first few real requests in logs

## Example Domains

| Domain | Credential that survives partial cleanup | Config locations to check |
|--------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| LLM gateway (OpenClaw, LiteLLM) | ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN, OPENAI_API_KEY | openclaw.json env, auth-profiles.json, oauth.json, systemd |
| Stripe integration | STRIPE_SECRET_KEY | .env, config.json, systemd, k8s secret |
| Database credentials | DB_PASSWORD | .env, app.config.js, docker-compose.yml, CI secrets |
| OAuth app | CLIENT_SECRET | .env, config.yaml, provider dashboard, local keychain |
| SMS/WhatsApp API | TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN | .env, config.json, serverless.yml, PM2 env |

skills.name: Cron-Poll Continuous Deploy via git ls-remote SHA Check
skills.description: When GitHub Actions SSH-deploy and inbound webhooks are both unavailable (SSH port blocked from runners, VPS behind NAT/firewall, no webhook capability) — use a per-minute cron job on the target host that calls `git ls-remote` to peek the remote main SHA and only redeploys when it differs from a stored `.deployed-sha`. Re-uses the same script for both one-shot manual deploys and the cron loop, with a self-installing `INSTALL_CRON=1` mode so the user runs one command and gets continuous deploy forever.
skills.body:
# Cron-Poll Continuous Deploy via git ls-remote SHA Check

## Problem

You want every `git push` to land on the production host within a minute, but:

- **GitHub Actions SSH-deploy doesn't work** — managed VPS providers (Hostinger, OVH, etc.) often filter inbound SSH from non-whitelisted IPs, and GitHub runner IPs change constantly.
- **GitHub webhooks can't reach the host** — the VPS is behind NAT, behind a corporate firewall, or has no public webhook endpoint configured.
- **Self-hosted runners are overkill** — for a static-files / scripts deploy, spinning up a runner just to copy files is silly.
- **Manual `git pull` is forgettable** — half the bug reports turn out to be "you forgot to deploy."

## Pattern — Per-minute cron polls the remote SHA

```bash
* * * * * /usr/local/bin/myapp-deploy.sh >> /var/log/myapp-deploy.log 2>&1
```

The script does a cheap `git ls-remote` (one HTTP round-trip, no clone) and exits silently when there's no new commit. When a new commit arrives, it clones shallow, syncs files, and writes the new SHA so the next tick is a no-op.

### The cheap remote SHA peek

```bash
REMOTE_SHA="$(git ls-remote "$REPO_URL" main | awk '{print $1}')"
LOCAL_SHA="$(cat "$TARGET/.deployed-sha" 2>/dev/null || true)"
if [ "$REMOTE_SHA" = "$LOCAL_SHA" ]; then
  exit 0    # silent — keeps cron output clean for emails/logs
fi
```

`git ls-remote` is ~30 KB of HTTP per minute. Negligible. No clone, no full fetch, no auth required for public repos.

### The self-installing mode

The same script handles both the deploy and its own cron registration. One env-flag gate is the whole trick:

```bash
if [ "${INSTALL_CRON:-0}" = "1" ]; then
  SCRIPT_PATH="/usr/local/bin/myapp-deploy.sh"
  curl -sL "$RAW_BASE/deploy.sh" -o "$SCRIPT_PATH"
  chmod +x "$SCRIPT_PATH"
  CRON_LINE="* * * * * $SCRIPT_PATH >> /var/log/myapp-deploy.log 2>&1"
  ( crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'myapp-deploy.sh' ; echo "$CRON_LINE" ) | crontab -
  echo "✓ cron installed"
  exit 0
fi
```

Now the user runs **one command, ever**:

```
curl -sL <raw>/deploy.sh | INSTALL_CRON=1 bash
```

…and from then on every `git push` auto-deploys.

## Full template

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

TARGET="${TARGET_DIR:-/var/www/myapp}"
REPO_URL="https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git"
RAW_BASE="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<org>/<repo>/main"
SUBDIR="path/to/app"        # use "." for repo-root apps
LOG="${LOG_PATH:-/var/log/myapp-deploy.log}"

# ── self-install cron (one-time) ───────────────────────────────────────────
if [ "${INSTALL_CRON:-0}" = "1" ]; then
  SP=/usr/local/bin/myapp-deploy.sh
  curl -sL "$RAW_BASE/path/to/deploy.sh" -o "$SP" && chmod +x "$SP"
  CRON="* * * * * TARGET_DIR=$TARGET $SP >> $LOG 2>&1"
  ( crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'myapp-deploy.sh' ; echo "$CRON" ) | crontab -
  echo "✓ cron installed: $CRON"
  exit 0
fi

# ── only-on-change SHA check ───────────────────────────────────────────────
REMOTE_SHA="$(git ls-remote "$REPO_URL" main 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')"
LOCAL_SHA="$(cat "$TARGET/.deployed-sha" 2>/dev/null || true)"
[ -n "$REMOTE_SHA" ] && [ "$REMOTE_SHA" = "$LOCAL_SHA" ] && exit 0

# ── deploy ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TMPDIR="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/myapp-deploy-$$"
trap 'rm -rf "$TMPDIR"' EXIT
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
git clone --depth 1 --quiet "$REPO_URL" "$TMPDIR/repo"
SRC="$TMPDIR/repo/$SUBDIR/"
[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "ERROR: $SUBDIR missing in repo"; exit 2; }

if command -v rsync >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  rsync -av --backup --suffix=.bak "$SRC" "$TARGET/"
else
  cp -av "$SRC." "$TARGET/"
fi

echo "$REMOTE_SHA" > "$TARGET/.deployed-sha"
echo "✓ DEPLOYED $(date '+%F %T %Z')  sha=${REMOTE_SHA:0:8}"
```

## Why this works where alternatives don't

| Approach | Needs SSH-in? | Needs webhook-in? | Needs CI budget? | Setup cost | Latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions + SSH | Yes | No | Yes | High (secrets, runner config) | ~30 s |
| GitHub Webhook + listener | No | Yes | No | Medium (HTTP server, secrets) | ~5 s |
| Manual `git pull` | No | No | No | Low | Forgotten |
| **Cron poll + ls-remote** | **No** | **No** | **No** | **One curl command** | **≤60 s** |

The `git ls-remote` poll is the single trick that makes the cron approach cheap. Without it (e.g., naive `git fetch && git diff` every minute) you'd be making real fetches all day.

## Generalization — when this fits

| Domain | Why it fits |
|---|---|
| Static site on managed VPS | No build step; rsync is the deploy |
| Internal admin panel behind firewall | Webhook can't reach the host |
| Edge / IoT device pulling app updates | Already polling-based by nature |
| Air-gapped staging where outbound HTTPS is allowed | Outbound poll fine; inbound blocked |
| Hobby projects with no CI budget | Free, simple, persistent |

## Anti-patterns

- **Don't** poll without the SHA check — running a clone every minute is wasteful and noisy in logs.
- **Don't** use `*/5 * * * *` to "save resources" — `git ls-remote` costs less than the cron daemon's own wakeup. 1-minute granularity is the right default.
- **Don't** fetch into the live target dir — clone to a tmpdir and rsync in, so a partial clone never half-replaces the live site.
- **Don't** silently swallow errors — pipe stderr to the log file, or one bad clone leaves you wondering why deploys silently stopped.
- **Don't** forget to dedupe the cron line on re-install — `grep -v <script-name>` before adding the line keeps `crontab -l` clean across reinstalls.

## Companion skills

- For the initial **bootstrap** of `deploy.sh` onto the VPS through a browser console where long pasted commands wrap and break, see `browser-console-curl-bash-deploy`. That skill solves *getting the file there once*; this skill solves *keeping it firing forever*.

The proposal then reads as Company B's document while still benefiting from Company A's mature template. version: 1.0.0 tags: [proposals, branding, multi-entity, group-companies, html-pdf, logos, wordmark] ``` ## Problem A consulting / agency / group operates two or more legal entities that share a back office and a design system. One entity has a polished proposal template (proven layout, brand CSS, signed-and-delivered samples in a canonical repo). The OTHER entity needs to send a proposal — same look-and-feel, but it cannot carry the first entity's logos because it would mis-represent the sender. Common situation: a Dubai parent + an Indian sister entity, a tech firm + a domain-licensed subsidiary, a partner-led agency where each partner has their own legal vehicle. The "house style" exists, but it belongs to the parent brand, not to the sending entity. If you blindly copy the parent's template you end up with a document that says "From: Subsidiary B" in the cover meta but has Parent A's logo in every footer band. That's confusing at best and brand-misleading at worst. ## Solution Separate **style** from **identity** and handle them independently: 1. **Reuse the style fully** — colours, typography, `.page` sizing, section structure, deliverable card layout, timeline dots. All CSS untouched. 2. **Strip the style-owner's logos** — remove every `` that carried the parent brand mark (cover icon, footer wordmark, header lockup). Do not try to embed both — that compounds confusion. 3. **Replace with typeset wordmark for the actual sender** — render the sender name as styled text using the same colour palette, so the document still has a brand presence in the cover and footer slots. 4. **Keep the sender's contact details in the contact lines** — addresses, emails, phone, signatory — all from the sender entity, never the style owner. ### Pattern: Cover wordmark replacement ```html
Sender Name
``` ```css .cover-wordmark { font-size: 16px; font-weight: 800; color: white; letter-spacing: 5px; text-transform: uppercase; margin-bottom: 14px; position: relative; z-index: 2; } .cover-wordmark span { color: var(--accent); } ``` ### Pattern: Footer wordmark replacement ```html
Sender Name
``` ```css .footer-left .f-wordmark { font-size: 13px; font-weight: 800; color: white; letter-spacing: 3px; text-transform: uppercase; } .footer-left .f-wordmark span { color: var(--accent); } ``` ### Why text over image - No risk of accidentally shipping the wrong brand's asset. - No base64 PNG bloat — file size drops dramatically (this session: 174 KB → 32 KB). - Renders identically on every machine — no font-emoji-renderer dependency. - If the sender later acquires a real logo asset, swap the `
` for an `` in one place. ## Example Domains | Domain | Style-owner (Company A) | Sender (Company B) | Why | |--------|------------------------|--------------------|---| | IT consulting group | Dubai parent FZE | Indian subsidiary Pvt Ltd | Local entity bills the Indian client | | Law firm partners | The firm | Individual partner LLP | Partner-led engagement | | Marketing agency | Holding company | White-labelled brand | Client must see white-label sender | | Healthcare network | Hospital trust | Owned diagnostic lab | Lab bills separately | | SaaS reseller | Original product brand | Authorised reseller | Reseller is the contract signer | | Architecture firm | Multi-discipline parent | Specialist studio (interiors) | Studio invoices for fit-out | ## Field-by-field checklist | Field | Source | |-------|--------| | `.page` CSS sizing (210×297mm) | **Style owner** | | Colour palette (--navy, --gold, etc.) | **Style owner** | | Section layout (cover / exec summary / scope / reports / timeline / terms) | **Style owner** | | Logos & marks (cover icon, footer wordmark) | **REMOVED — replace with text wordmark for sender** | | Cover-meta "Prepared By" | **Sender** | | Cover-meta "Prepared For" | **Recipient** | | Footer contact (email, phone, address) | **Sender** | | Footer right "client" line | **Recipient** | | Doc number prefix | **Sender's prefix** (e.g. `BSL-` for Betser, not `BTR-` for Bettroi) | | Signatory block (left) | **Sender's signatory** | | Signatory block (right) | **Recipient** (generic if no named individual provided) | | Confidential strip | **Sender's copyright** | | Terms & conditions language (validity, IP, NDA reference) | **Sender's standard terms** | ## Anti-patterns - **Both logos on cover**: tries to "show partnership" but reads as a confused brand sandwich. Pick one — the sender — and present the document as their own. - **Parent's wordmark in footer, child's address line above it**: makes the address-block look like a sub-tenant of the parent. Same fix: pure-text wordmark for the sender. - **Mixing colour palettes**: do not introduce a second accent colour for the sender if the style already has one. The style owner's palette stays intact. - **Doc number with style-owner's prefix**: don't use `PARENT-2026-####` when the contract will be invoiced by `SUBSIDIARY-2026-####`. The prefix follows the sender, not the style. - **Leaving the canonical CLAUDE.md's "Mandatory logos" rule in force**: the style owner's CLAUDE.md says BOTH logos are mandatory — but that rule applies to documents AUTHORED BY the style owner. When sender is different, the rule is satisfied by the text-wordmark replacement; don't try to honour the literal "embed JPEG + embed PNG" instruction. ## Variations - **Sender has its own logo asset.** Once Company B commissions a real wordmark, replace the typeset `
` with an `` in the cover-wordmark and footer-wordmark slots. CSS stays the same — give the `` the same height as the text version was. - **Co-branded engagement (legal requirement).** Some regulated industries require both entities' marks. In that case use a *small* "Delivered with [Parent Name]" line in the cover-meta, never two competing logos in the brand zones. - **Internal-only or draft-stage document.** Pre-signature drafts can carry the style-owner's logos for working purposes; strip them at the final-version step. ## Key Rule **Style and identity are independent. Reuse style fully; replace identity completely. Use text-only wordmarks when you don't have the sender's logo file — never silently keep the style-owner's mark in a document the style-owner did not send.**

skills.name: Custom Slash Command — Encode Multi-Step Protocols
skills.description: Create custom Claude Code slash commands in ~/.claude/commands/ that invoke repeatable multi-step workflows with $ARGUMENTS substitution — so any protocol can be triggered with /command-name <target> instead of pasting prompts.
skills.body:
# Custom Slash Command — Encode Multi-Step Protocols

## Problem

You have a multi-step protocol (integration workflow, code review checklist, security audit, deployment sequence) that you want to invoke consistently. Pasting the full prompt each time is error-prone, inconsistent, and easy to forget.

## Solution

Create a Markdown file in `~/.claude/commands/` — it becomes a slash command available in every Claude Code session. Use `$ARGUMENTS` to pass a target (feature name, file path, module, etc.) at call time.

---

## Setup

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude/commands
# Create your command file:
touch ~/.claude/commands/your-command-name.md
```

Command is immediately available as `/your-command-name` in any Claude Code session.

---

## File Format

```markdown
# ~/.claude/commands/zero-hardcode.md

We are starting a new feature: **$ARGUMENTS**

Follow the Zero-Hardcode Protocol strictly. Do not skip steps.

**STEP 1 — Backend + Schema (do this now, nothing else)**
- Create the Prisma model / DB table / API route
- Do NOT touch React, Zustand, or any UI file yet
- Output: schema + service code only

When done, tell me: "Step 1 complete. Run: [exact verification command]"

**STEP 2 — Wait**
I will run the verification. Paste real output before proceeding.

**STEP 3 — Store** (only after Step 2 confirmed)
...

Start with Step 1 now.
```

---

## Usage

```
/zero-hardcode Live PLC Tag Dashboard
/zero-hardcode BNI Contact Status Table  
/zero-hardcode WhatsApp Message History
/security-audit components/PaymentForm.tsx
/deploy-checklist production
```

`$ARGUMENTS` is replaced with everything typed after the command name.

---

## Command File Locations

| Path | Scope |
|------|-------|
| `~/.claude/commands/name.md` | Global — every project |
| `<project>/.claude/commands/name.md` | Project-only |

---

## Anatomy of a Good Command File

```markdown
# Short context sentence with $ARGUMENTS

[What to do — imperative, no hedging]

**STEP 1 — [Name] (do this first, nothing else)**
- Specific instruction
- What NOT to do yet
- Expected output format

"When done, say: '[specific phrase]'"   ← Gate phrase to control pacing

**STEP 2 — [Name] (only after I confirm Step 1)**
...

Start with Step 1 now.   ← End with the trigger
```

Key elements:
- **Gate phrases** — "only after I confirm", "wait for my output" — prevent the AI from skipping ahead
- **Explicit prohibitions** — "Do NOT touch the UI yet" — prevents premature work
- **Expected output format** — tells Claude what a completed step looks like
- **`$ARGUMENTS`** — the target the user names at call time

---

## Multi-Command Pattern — Build a Protocol Library

```
~/.claude/commands/
├── zero-hardcode.md      # /zero-hardcode <feature>
├── security-audit.md     # /security-audit <file>
├── deploy-checklist.md   # /deploy-checklist <env>
├── code-review.md        # /code-review <PR description>
├── db-migration.md       # /db-migration <table change>
└── onboard-intern.md     # /onboard-intern <name>
```

---

## Example Domains

| Use Case | Command |
|----------|---------|
| SCADA feature build | `/zero-hardcode Live Tag HMI Panel` |
| Security review before PR | `/security-audit src/api/auth.ts` |
| Deployment gates | `/deploy-checklist staging` |
| Intern onboarding day | `/onboard-intern Day 2 — Claude SDK` |
| DB schema change | `/db-migration add phone column to contacts` |
| API endpoint design | `/api-design POST /v1/contacts/bulk` |

skills.name: custom-domain-wrong-project-404
skills.description: A custom domain returns 404 (or serves stale features) on routes that demonstrably exist in your current codebase, because the domain is attached to a DIFFERENT, older platform project than the one your code deploys to. Use when "the route exists in my repo but 404s in production", when two similarly-named projects exist on the host (e.g. "myapp" and "myapp.com"), or after a domain was recently added/migrated.
skills.body:
# Custom Domain Pointing at the Wrong Project (Stale 404s)

A hosting account can contain multiple projects with confusingly similar names
(`myapp` vs `myapp.com`). A custom domain is bound to exactly one project. If the
domain is bound to an **older/stale** project while your code auto-deploys to a
**different** project, production serves the old build: new routes 404, new features
are missing, env vars you set on the "right" project never apply.

## Tell-tale signature

- A route 404s on the live domain but **exists** in your repo.
- The same route returns **401/200 (not 404)** on the current project's
  `*.platform.app` preview URL — proving the route exists there, just not on the domain.
- Env-var changes on "the project" have no effect (you edited the wrong project).
- Two projects with near-identical names show up in the project list.

> 404 = route genuinely absent (wrong/old build). 401 or auth-wall = route present
> but protected. Use this distinction to tell "missing code" from "blocked access".

## Diagnose: which project backs the domain?

```bash
# Vercel: resolves the domain to its serving deployment + project name
vercel inspect <domain>          # look at the "name" / project field

# Confirm which project your local repo deploys to
cat .vercel/project.json         # projectId + projectName that git push targets
```

If `vercel inspect <domain>` shows a project name different from
`.vercel/project.json`, the domain is on the wrong project.

## Fix: move the domain to the correct project

CLI prompts for domain removal are often un-pipeable; the REST API is reliable.
Fetch the platform token from the CLI's credential file, then remove + add:

```bash
TOKEN=$(python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('$HOME/Library/Application Support/com.vercel.cli/auth.json'))['token'])")
TEAM=team_xxx

# Remove from the OLD/wrong project
curl -s -X DELETE "https://api.vercel.com/v9/projects/$OLD_PID/domains/$DOMAIN?teamId=$TEAM" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Add to the CORRECT project (the one .vercel/project.json points to)
curl -s -X POST "https://api.vercel.com/v10/projects/$NEW_PID/domains?teamId=$TEAM" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"name\":\"$DOMAIN\"}"
```

Then move every related host too — **don't forget the `www.` (or other) subdomain**;
it is a separate domain entry and is easy to leave behind on the old project. After
moving, trigger a production deploy on the correct project so the alias attaches to a
fresh build.

## Gotcha: deployment protection vs. custom domains

If the project has SSO/password "deployment protection", the `*.platform.app` URLs may
return 401 while the **custom domain still works** — many platforms exempt custom
domains (`deploymentType: all_except_custom_domains`). Don't mistake a protected
preview URL's 401 for a broken domain; test the actual custom domain.

## Example Domains

| Host | "which project backs the domain?" | Move domain |
|------|-----------------------------------|-------------|
| Vercel | `vercel inspect <domain>` → project name | REST `DELETE`/`POST .../domains` |
| Netlify | Site settings → Domain management | reassign domain to correct site |
| Cloudflare Pages | Pages project → Custom domains | detach + attach on the right project |
| Render | Service → Custom domains | move domain between services |

## Verify

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://$DOMAIN/the-new-route   # expect 200
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://www.$DOMAIN/the-new-route
```

skills.name: document-type-discipline-plan-vs-proposal
skills.body:
# Document-Type Discipline — Plan vs Proposal vs Scope vs Spec

## Skill Metadata
```yaml
name: Document-Type Discipline — Plan vs Proposal vs Scope vs Spec
description: The first word of a document's title (Proposal / Project Plan / Scope Document / Technical Specification / Statement of Work) commits the writer to a specific vocabulary, signatory model, validity model and section structure. Mis-labelling a document forces dozens of downstream wording errors. Before drafting any client-facing artefact, name its type explicitly and let that drive every word.
version: 1.0.0
tags: [documents, proposals, project-plans, scope, copywriting, governance, framing]
```

## Problem

A writer (or an LLM) starts drafting "a document for the client" without nailing down its type. They reach for the most familiar template — usually a Proposal — and produce paragraphs full of "we propose…", "this proposal is valid for 60 days…", "Prepared For / Prepared By". The client then reads it and says:

> "Wait, this isn't a proposal. We already chose the vendor. This is supposed to be the project plan."

Now the writer has to scrub every instance of "proposal", "proposes", "valid until", "prepared by" — typically 15–30 distinct edits across cover, headers, page-nav band, terms section, and signature blocks. Worse: subtle framing leaks remain — "Executive Summary" instead of "Project Brief", "Scope of Work" instead of "Project Scope", "Terms & Conditions" instead of "Governance & Engagement Terms" — and these sneak through because they LOOK template-correct.

The root cause is naming the document type AFTER drafting instead of BEFORE.

## Solution

Make document-type the FIRST decision. Pick the type from a short canonical list before opening the template. Each type has its own wordbook — never mix them.

### The four common types

| Type | Used when | Implied stance |
|------|-----------|---------------|
| **Proposal** | The vendor is competing for / not yet awarded the work. Sales document. | "Pick us — here's why and what it costs." |
| **Project Plan** | Vendor is already chosen. Document operationalises the engagement. | "Here is how the work will run." |
| **Scope Document / SoW** | The commercial decision is made; this defines what is and isn't in. | "Here is precisely what is included." |
| **Technical Specification** | Audience is engineering, not commercial. | "Here is how it will be built." |

Two more, less common but worth recognising:
- **Discovery Report** — output of a paid discovery phase, precedes any proposal.
- **Change Request / Amendment** — modifies an existing scope or plan.

### Vocabulary table — never mix across columns

| Concept | Proposal | Project Plan | Scope Doc / SoW | Technical Spec |
|---------|----------|--------------|-----------------|----------------|
| Verb of intent | "proposes" | "will deliver" | "covers" / "includes" | "implements" |
| Cover label | "Technical Proposal" | "Project Plan" | "Statement of Work" | "Technical Specification" |
| Validity clause | "Valid for 60 days" | (none — versioned) | (none — annexed to contract) | (none — versioned) |
| Cover-meta column 1 | "Prepared For" | "Client" | "Client" | "Owner" |
| Cover-meta column 2 | "Prepared By" | "Project Sponsor" | "Vendor" | "Author / Architect" |
| Cover-meta column 3 | "Reference" | "Plan Code" | "SoW Number" | "Spec Reference" |
| Cover-meta column 4 | "Valid Until" | "Effective Date" + version | "Effective Date" | "Version" |
| Section 1 heading | "Executive Summary" | "Project Brief" | "Engagement Overview" | "System Overview" |
| Section 2 heading | "Scope of Work" | "Project Scope / Workstreams" | "Deliverables" | "Functional Requirements" |
| Section 6 heading | "Commercials" / "Pricing" | "Acceptance Milestones" | "Deliverables Schedule" | "Acceptance Tests" |
| Section 7 heading | "Terms & Conditions" | "Governance & Engagement Terms" | "Commercial Terms" | "Non-functional Requirements" |
| Signature block label | "For [Client] / For [Vendor]" | "Project Sponsor / Client Representative" | "Authorised Signatory each side" | "Author / Approver" |
| Signature line tag | "Signature & Date" | "Approval Signature & Date" | "Counter-signature & Date" | "Reviewer Sign-off" |
| Closing footer note | "Confidential — Proposal" | "Confidential — Project Plan" | "Confidential — Contract Annex" | "Confidential — Internal" |

### Pre-write checklist (60-second discipline)

1. **State the type aloud**: "I am writing a [Project Plan]." If you can't say it in one of the four words above, you have not decided yet — stop and decide.
2. **Audit the template**: open the template and search-replace its document-type words before changing any content. If the template was a Proposal and your output is a Project Plan, fix every column header and section badge FIRST.
3. **Write a grep gate**: before the final render, run `grep -i "proposal\|valid until\|prepared by"` (the words from the wrong type). If any match in your output, you have a leak.
4. **Filename mirrors type**: `Foo_ProjectPlan_REF.html` not `Foo_Proposal_REF.html` (or the other way round). The filename is the loudest signal.

### Re-label retrofit — when you discover mid-drafting that the type is wrong

This happened in the originating session. The user said "this is not a proposal, it is a project plan" after 30 sentences had already been drafted. Recovery:

1. Update the doc title and filename first.
2. Do a single Edit pass on cover label, cover-meta column headings, and page-nav band — the high-visibility leaks.
3. Do a vocabulary pass on body content using the table above.
4. Add or delete sections that exist only in one type (Validity clause exists in Proposal, doesn't in Project Plan — delete it).
5. Final grep gate: `grep -i "propos\|valid until\|prepared by"` should return empty.
6. Rename signature blocks and tag-lines.

The retrofit is faster than a re-draft if you treat it as a typed pipeline of edits, not a rewrite.

## Example Domains

| Domain | Wrong label that gets reached for | Correct label | Why it matters |
|--------|----------------------------------|---------------|---------------|
| Software consulting | "Proposal" used after award letter signed | "Project Plan" | Implies commercial decision is open — invites renegotiation |
| Architecture firm | "Concept Note" used for tender response | "Design Proposal" | Concept note isn't biddable; tender needs price and validity |
| Marketing agency | "Strategy Document" used for retainer SOW | "Statement of Work" | Strategy doc is advisory; SOW is the contractual instrument |
| Law firm | "Engagement Letter" used for internal matter plan | "Matter Plan" | Engagement letter is client-facing fee terms; matter plan is internal |
| Healthcare | "Treatment Plan" used for hospital admission summary | "Discharge Summary" | Each has regulatory templates; cross-naming triggers audit issues |
| Cybersecurity | "Pentest Report" used for vulnerability advisory | "Security Advisory" | Pentest report has scoped findings; advisory is open recommendations |
| Construction | "Quote" used for change order | "Variation Order" | Quote is pre-contract; variation is post-contract amendment |

## Anti-patterns

- **Copying a recent template without checking its type.** If your last document was a Proposal and you copy its structure for what is actually a Project Plan, you inherit thirty wording mistakes.
- **Drafting the body before the type label.** The label drives the body. Decide first.
- **Mixing types within one document** ("This proposal/plan…"). Means the writer hasn't decided. Pick one.
- **Letting the cover say "Project Plan" but the inside say "we propose".** Visible header passes a quick review; inside vocabulary leaks during a careful read.
- **Carrying a Validity clause into a Project Plan.** Plans are versioned, not date-validated. Replace with "This Project Plan is Version 1.0; subsequent revisions issued as new versions with a change log."
- **Leaving "Prepared By / Prepared For" on a Project Plan.** Replace with "Project Sponsor / Client" — the role-language matches the post-award stance.

## When the right answer is "both"

Sometimes a client needs the SAME content delivered as both a Proposal (for procurement) and a Project Plan (for execution). The correct response is two documents with different framings — never one mongrel. Re-use only the content blocks (deliverables, timeline, terms) and rewrite the framing (cover, signatures, validity, headings) for each.

## Key Rule

**Name the document type as the first decision. Let the type drive every word, header, signature, and validity clause. Never mix vocabularies across types. Re-labelling mid-draft is fast IF you treat it as a typed pipeline of edits, not a rewrite.**

skills.name: Dual-Publish Reusable Setup Guide as Local Skill + Standalone Public Repo
skills.description: When the user asks to save procedural how-to content "for next time," publish it in two places at once - as a harvested SKILL.md (auto-loads in future agent sessions via the skill catalog) AND as a standalone public GitHub repo (shareable, indexable, install-from-anywhere). The repo leads its README with a plain-English intro for non-technical readers, then the technical setup. Includes an idempotent setup.sh and an .env.example.
skills.body:
# Dual-Publish Reusable Setup Guide

## When to use

The user has just walked through a non-trivial setup procedure (env-var configuration,
provider redirect, CLI install, OAuth dance, deploy bootstrap, etc.) and asks any of:

- "save this as a memory/skill for next time"
- "remember how to do this"
- "save it in github as a repo"
- "make this reusable"

A single artifact (memory entry OR file in current project) is the wrong answer. Memory
is for who-the-user-is / project context; ephemeral files in a working directory get
buried. Procedural how-tos belong somewhere reusable across machines and sessions.

## Pattern

Publish the same content in **both** of these places:

### 1. Local harvested skill (auto-loaded in future sessions)

Path: `~/.claude/skills/harvested/<slug>/SKILL.md`

- Frontmatter (`name`, `description`, `type`, `tags`) so the catalog injector picks it up
- Domain-neutral language (no client-specific names, no project paths)
- Example Domains table at the bottom showing where the pattern applies
- The skill catalog regenerates on session start, so no manual index edit needed

### 2. Standalone public GitHub repo

Path: `<user>/<slug>` on GitHub, working dir `/tmp/<slug>/` (NOT inside another project)

- `README.md` with a **plain-English intro at the top**, technical setup below
- `SKILL.md` (exact copy of the harvested skill, frontmatter intact) so the repo itself
  is importable as a skill by anyone who clones it
- `setup.sh` - idempotent installer (see related skill: marker-based rc dedupe)
- `.env.example` - the env vars with placeholder values, no secrets
- `.gitignore` - block `.env`, `*.bak.*`, `.DS_Store`

Publish via `gh repo create <owner>/<slug> --public --source=. --push`.

## Why two places, not one

| Place | Strength | Weakness |
|-------|----------|----------|
| Local skill only | Auto-loads in future sessions, zero friction | Tied to one machine; can't share via URL |
| GitHub repo only | Shareable, indexable, installable from any machine | Won't surface in agent context unless cloned |
| **Both** | Future-self gets it free; future-others get a URL | One-time duplication cost |

The community sync layer (Ironbark) already pushes harvested skills to a community repo
on a 30-min cron, but a standalone repo is preferable when the artifact is a
self-contained product that benefits from its own README, install script, releases, and
star count. Skills are catalog entries; repos are products.

## README structure (top-down)

```
# <Product Name>

<one-sentence value prop>

---

## For non-tech readers: what is this?

<plain-English explanation, no jargon, simple before/after diagram>

---

## Quick start (one-liner)

git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && bash setup.sh

---

## Manual setup

<step-by-step technical instructions>
```

The plain-English section answers four questions: what is this, why bother, what's the
catch, what are the moving pieces. Use a before/after ASCII diagram if a flow change
is involved.

## Verification checklist before declaring done

1. Local skill: `cat ~/.claude/skills/harvested/<slug>/SKILL.md` shows frontmatter and
   body; on next session start it appears in the project's `CLAUDE.md` catalog table.
2. GitHub repo: `gh repo view <owner>/<slug> --json url,visibility` returns
   `"visibility":"PUBLIC"` and a working URL.
3. Open the repo URL in a browser - README renders, file tree is correct, no committed
   secrets.

## Example Domains

| Domain | Slug pattern | Notes |
|--------|--------------|-------|
| LLM provider redirect (Claude Code -> DeepSeek, OpenAI-compatible proxy, LiteLLM) | `<cli>-<provider>-backend` | Original case that produced this skill |
| OAuth headless setup (gcloud, gh, gcalendar via SSH tunnel) | `<service>-headless-auth` | Reuses idempotent shell-rc dedupe skill |
| VPS bootstrap (curl-bash deploy, systemd service install) | `<service>-vps-bootstrap` | README plain-English section explains "what runs where" |
| CLI install + env-config combo (anthropic-sdk, vercel, supabase) | `<cli>-quickstart` | setup.sh dedupes if user re-runs |
| Hardware/IoT device provisioning (OpenWrt, Raspberry Pi, edge agent) | `<device>-provision` | README must explain physical steps non-techies skip |

## Anti-patterns

- Saving as a memory entry only - memory is for personal/project context, not reusable procedures.
- Putting the guide inside an unrelated project's `docs/` folder - it gets lost.
- One README written for engineers only - non-technical stakeholders can't share the link with their team.
- A repo without `setup.sh` - users hand-copy commands, miss steps, blame the guide.
- Committing the actual API key in `.env` instead of `.env.example` - unrecoverable leak.

skills.name: env-var-secret-newline-and-redeploy-snapshot
skills.description: Two silent traps when setting platform secrets from the CLI — `echo` appends a trailing newline that breaks exact-match secrets (passwords, tokens, API keys), and a "redeploy" reuses the old env-var snapshot instead of picking up changed values. Use when a credential/secret stored as an env var is rejected ("invalid credentials") even though the value looks correct, or when an env-var change doesn't take effect after redeploying.
skills.body:
# Env-Var Secret: Trailing Newline + Redeploy Snapshot Traps

Two independent, easy-to-miss failure modes when storing a secret as a platform
environment variable (Vercel, Netlify, Railway, Fly, Cloud Run, GitHub Actions, etc.)
and consuming it at runtime for an **exact string comparison** (password, bearer token,
API key, HMAC secret, webhook signature).

## Symptom

A secret stored as an env var is rejected at runtime — "invalid credentials",
401, signature mismatch — even though printing the value shows the right characters.
Or: you change the env var, redeploy, and the old behaviour persists.

## Trap 1 — `echo` appends a trailing newline

`echo "secret" | <cli> env add KEY` stores `secret\n`, not `secret`. The newline is
invisible in most output and survives encryption. Any exact-match consumer fails.

```bash
# WRONG — stores a trailing \n
echo "$VALUE" | vercel env add MY_SECRET production

# RIGHT — no newline
printf '%s' "$VALUE" | vercel env add MY_SECRET production
```

**Verify byte-for-byte** (don't trust visual inspection — a trailing `\n` often just
looks like the value ending on its own line):

```bash
# Pull the decrypted value and show its repr + length
<fetch value> | python3 -c "import sys; v=sys.stdin.read(); print(repr(v), len(v))"
# 'secret\n' len 7  <- BAD
# 'secret'   len 6  <- GOOD
```

If the CLI's interactive `add` resists scripting, PATCH the value through the
platform's REST API instead, which takes a clean JSON string with no shell echo:

```bash
curl -s -X PATCH "$API/projects/$PID/env/$ENV_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value":"secret"}'
```

## Trap 2 — "redeploy" reuses the old env-var snapshot

Many platforms capture env vars into an immutable snapshot at deploy-creation time.
A **redeploy of an existing deployment reuses that snapshot** — it does NOT read the
current env-var values. So after editing a secret, a redeploy can silently run with
the stale value.

Fix: trigger a **fresh build** (git push to the production branch, or a brand-new
deploy), not a redeploy of a prior build.

```bash
# Stale: reuses dpl_OLD's captured env vars
vercel redeploy <old-deployment-url> --target production

# Fresh: new build reads current env vars
git commit --allow-empty -m "Redeploy to pick up changed secret" && git push
```

## Isolation tactic that pinpoints both

When a credential is rejected, test the credential **directly against the upstream
service**, bypassing your app's env-var plumbing:

```bash
# Does the raw email/password actually authenticate?
curl -s -X POST "$AUTH_URL/token?grant_type=password" \
  -H "apikey: $ANON" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"user@x.com","password":"the-password"}'
```

- Direct call **succeeds**, app **fails** → the bug is in the env-var value (newline)
  or which deployment is running (stale snapshot), NOT the credential itself.
- Direct call **fails** → the credential is genuinely wrong (reset it at the source).

This split halves the search space before you touch any config.

## Example Domains

| Platform / secret | "echo newline" risk | "redeploy snapshot" risk |
|-------------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Vercel env var holding an auth password | `echo \| vercel env add` adds `\n` | `vercel redeploy` reuses old snapshot |
| Netlify build env API token | `echo \| netlify env:set` | redeploy of pinned build keeps old value |
| GitHub Actions secret (HMAC key) | `echo \| gh secret set` adds `\n` | re-run of old workflow run uses old secret |
| Railway / Fly secret | `echo \| railway variables set` | restart vs. fresh deploy distinction |
| `.env` file written with `echo "x" >> .env` | trailing `\n` per line | n/a |

## Checklist

1. Set secrets with `printf '%s'`, never bare `echo`.
2. After setting, fetch the decrypted value and assert `len` matches the expected length.
3. To apply a changed secret, force a fresh build (git push), not a redeploy.
4. If a credential is rejected, test it directly against the upstream API first to
   decide whether the fault is the value, the deployment, or the credential.

skills.name: Exhaustive Error Hunting — Never Stop at the First Fix
skills.description: When debugging a broken feature, NEVER assume the first error found is the only one. Systematically trace the entire data path and fix ALL breakpoints before declaring success.
skills.body:
# Exhaustive Error Hunting — Never Stop at the First Fix

## The Anti-Pattern: Fix One Thing, Declare Victory

When a feature doesn't work, we find one error, fix it, deploy, and ask the user to test. The user reports it still doesn't work. We find another error, fix it, deploy again. Repeat 10 times. Each round-trip wastes 10-15 minutes of the user's time.

## The Real-World Example (NexaProc tag values showing --)

We spent 2 hours fixing "tag value shows --" across 8 separate deployments because we fixed errors one at a time instead of tracing the entire chain upfront:

| Round | Error Found | Deployed? | Still Broken? |
|-------|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| 1 | Polling not started | Yes | Yes |
| 2 | PM2 cluster splits state | Yes | Yes |
| 3 | Socket.IO room subscription missing | Yes | Yes |
| 4 | `io.to(room).emit` needs `io.emit` broadcast | Yes | Yes |
| 5 | `hasRealData` check too strict | Yes | Yes |
| 6 | `WS_URL` defaults to localhost in production | Yes | **FINALLY WORKED** |

Error #6 was the ROOT CAUSE all along. If we had traced the full chain first, we would have found it in 5 minutes.

## The Correct Methodology

### Step 1: Map the ENTIRE data path

Before fixing anything, trace from source to destination:

```
Source: PLC simulator (%M0 coil)
  → VPN tunnel (WireGuard 10.100.0.2 → 10.100.0.1)
  → Modbus TCP read (polling engine on VPS)
  → Tag Engine (in-memory, emits tagChange)
  → Socket.IO (io.emit to connected clients)
  → nginx (reverse proxy, WebSocket upgrade)
  → Browser (Socket.IO client connects to WS_URL)
  → Realtime Store (Zustand, updates tagValues Map)
  → ScreenViewerPage (reads tagValues, applies to nodes)
  → UI (valve changes state/color)
```

### Step 2: Verify EACH link independently

For each link in the chain, verify it works:

```bash
# Link 1: Can VPS reach PLC?
ssh vps "nc -w 2 10.100.0.2 502 && echo OK"

# Link 2: Can Modbus read the coil?
ssh vps "node -e 'require(\"modbus-serial\")... readCoils(0,1)'"

# Link 3: Is polling engine running?
curl /api/polling/status

# Link 4: Is tag engine receiving values?
curl /api/polling/stats  # totalPolls > 0, goodQuality > 0

# Link 5: Is Socket.IO broadcasting?
grep "io.emit" dist/services/realtime.service.js

# Link 6: Is nginx proxying WebSocket?
Check nginx config for /socket.io/ proxy

# Link 7: What URL does the browser connect to?
Check WS_URL in constants.ts — IS IT LOCALHOST?!

# Link 8: Is the browser receiving events?
F12 → Network → WS tab → check for active WebSocket
```

### Step 3: Fix ALL broken links, then deploy ONCE

Don't deploy after each fix. Find ALL issues first, fix them all, deploy once, verify.

## Common Multi-Error Chains in SCADA/Fullstack Apps

### Chain 1: "Data doesn't show in UI"
1. Backend not reading from device (polling not started)
2. Backend reading but not broadcasting (Socket.IO room issue)
3. Broadcasting but wrong URL (WS_URL = localhost)
4. Right URL but client not subscribing (missing emit)
5. Subscribing but store not updating (wrong event name)
6. Store updating but UI not re-rendering (stale closure)

### Chain 2: "Login works but shows wrong user"
1. Real login succeeds (backend returns correct user)
2. But mock login fallback ALSO runs (catches non-401 errors)
3. Mock user overwrites real user in store
4. TopBar has HARDCODED "Operator" text (never reads from store)
5. localStorage has stale auth from previous session

### Chain 3: "CRUD saves but data disappears"
1. Create succeeds (API returns 201)
2. But list refresh fails (limit > backend max)
3. Page shows empty (user thinks create failed)
4. On reload, store initializes with mock data (not from API)
5. Screen store uses Zustand without persistence (lost on refresh)
6. Project ID is non-UUID string from old mock data

## The Rule

**When a feature is broken, trace the ENTIRE data path from source to UI before fixing anything. Verify each link. List ALL broken links. Fix them ALL. Deploy ONCE. Test ONCE.**

Never:
- Fix one thing and ask "try again"
- Assume the first error is the only error
- Deploy 8 times for one feature
- Blame stale cache when the real issue is a wrong URL

## Checklist Before Declaring "Fixed"

- [ ] Traced full data path from source to UI
- [ ] Verified each link independently with evidence
- [ ] Found ALL broken links (not just the first)
- [ ] Fixed all issues in one commit
- [ ] Deployed once
- [ ] Verified end-to-end with user
- [ ] Saved time by not doing 8 round-trips

skills.name: gh api Bulk Operations Without Zsh Glob Expansion Bugs
skills.description: When scripting `gh api` to POST/PATCH the same payload to many GitHub repos (bulk webhooks, branch-protection rules, repo settings), the `-f config[url]=...` flag with literal brackets crashes under zsh with `(eval): no matches found: events[]=push` — zsh treats the brackets as a glob. Fix by building the JSON body once as a string, then piping via stdin with `gh api -X POST <path> --input -`. Adds a skip-on-already-exists existence check, a progress dot stream, and a final summary so a 100+-repo loop is auditable.
skills.body:
# `gh api` Bulk Operations Without Zsh Glob Expansion Bugs

## Problem

You want to set up a webhook on every active repo in your GitHub org. The natural attempt is the example from `gh api --help`:

```bash
for repo in $(gh repo list myorg --json name --jq '.[].name'); do
  gh api -X POST "repos/myorg/$repo/hooks" \
    -f name=web \
    -F active=true \
    -f events[]=push \
    -f config[url]="https://example.com/hook" \
    -f config[content_type]=json \
    -f config[secret]="$SECRET"
done
```

…which under zsh dies on every iteration with:

```
(eval):19: no matches found: events[]=push
```

zsh treats `[` and `]` as glob characters. Without `setopt nonomatch`, an argument with brackets is rejected before `gh` even starts, because zsh tries to expand `events[]` as a filename pattern and finds no matches.

You can `setopt nonomatch` or `noglob`, but those silently change the rest of the script's behaviour. There's a cleaner fix.

## The fix — JSON via stdin

```bash
SECRET="..."
URL="https://example.com/hook"

# Build the payload once as a single JSON string
BODY=$(cat <<EOF
{
  "name": "web",
  "active": true,
  "events": ["push"],
  "config": {
    "url": "$URL",
    "content_type": "json",
    "secret": "$SECRET",
    "insecure_ssl": "0"
  }
}
EOF
)

# Loop — pipe the body via stdin, no bracket arguments
while read -r repo; do
  echo "$BODY" | gh api -X POST "repos/$repo/hooks" --input - --silent
done < repos.txt
```

`--input -` tells `gh` to read the request body from stdin, so no flags carry brackets and zsh has nothing to glob.

## Production-grade loop

For 100+ repos you want resilience and a clean summary:

```bash
SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
URL="https://example.com/hook"

BODY=$(cat <<EOF
{"name":"web","active":true,"events":["push"],"config":{"url":"$URL","content_type":"json","secret":"$SECRET","insecure_ssl":"0"}}
EOF
)

# Filter to active, admin-able, non-fork, non-archived repos
gh repo list --limit 500 \
  --json name,owner,isFork,isArchived,viewerPermission,pushedAt \
  --jq '[.[]
        | select(.isFork==false and .isArchived==false
                 and .viewerPermission=="ADMIN"
                 and .pushedAt > "2025-01-01")
        | "\(.owner.login)/\(.name)"][]' \
  > /tmp/repos.txt

added=0; skipped=0; failed=0
fail_log=()

while read -r repo; do
  [ -z "$repo" ] && continue

  # Skip if hook already exists (idempotent)
  existing=$(gh api "repos/$repo/hooks" \
    --jq '.[] | select(.config.url=="'"$URL"'") | .id' 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -n "$existing" ]; then skipped=$((skipped+1)); continue; fi

  if echo "$BODY" | gh api -X POST "repos/$repo/hooks" --input - --silent 2>/dev/null; then
    added=$((added+1))
    printf "."
  else
    failed=$((failed+1))
    fail_log+=("$repo")
    printf "x"
  fi

  # Progress every 25 repos
  if (( (added + skipped + failed) % 25 == 0 )); then
    printf " %d/%d\n" "$((added + skipped + failed))" "$(wc -l < /tmp/repos.txt)"
  fi
done < /tmp/repos.txt

echo
echo "=== summary ==="
echo "  added:   $added"
echo "  skipped: $skipped (already present)"
echo "  failed:  $failed"
[ ${#fail_log[@]} -gt 0 ] && printf '  - %s\n' "${fail_log[@]:0:10}"
```

Three things make this production-grade:

1. **Existence check** — re-running the loop is safe; already-configured repos don't get duplicate hooks.
2. **Progress dots and counters** — `.` for added, `x` for failed, count every 25 — you can tell at 30 seconds whether the loop is working at all.
3. **Failure list** — captures repo names that errored so you can retry them in isolation, instead of seeing only the count.

## Other shapes that hit the same trap

`gh api` flag-style command lines fail on zsh whenever an argument contains literal brackets:

```bash
gh api -f config[url]=...      # bracket in field name
gh api -f events[]=push        # bracket in field name
gh api -F branch_protection_rules[1][required_approving_review_count]=2
```

All three need the JSON-stdin treatment, or — if you really want flag-style — wrap each offending arg in single quotes inside zsh:

```bash
'-f' 'events[]=push'           # works because each token is fully quoted
```

But once you have nested keys (`config[secret]`, `branch_protection_rules[1][...]`), the JSON-stdin route is shorter and clearer.

## Generalization

Same pattern applies anywhere you script bulk operations against a JSON-API CLI:

| CLI | Bulk-edit example |
|---|---|
| `gh api` | Webhooks, branch protection, repo metadata, issue labels |
| `aws` | IAM-policy attach/detach across accounts |
| `gcloud` | IAM bindings across projects |
| `kubectl` | Apply same manifest to many namespaces |
| `gitlab` | Project hooks, CI variables across many projects |
| `vercel api` | Env-vars across projects |

Build the body once, pipe via stdin (`--input -` / `--data-binary @-` / `apply -f -`), loop with skip-on-exists.

## Anti-patterns

- **Don't** `setopt nonomatch` to "fix" zsh — it changes the rest of the script's behaviour silently. Pipe-stdin is local and explicit.
- **Don't** echo a single mega-payload with `$()` substitution and trust that special chars survive. Use `cat <<EOF` heredoc with no interpolation tokens like `$()` inside, or quote your secrets carefully.
- **Don't** rely on `gh api` exit code = 0 alone — always `2>/dev/null` to suppress GitHub's per-repo error noise from the loop and capture failures into a `fail_log` array, otherwise a 5% failure rate looks like a successful run.
- **Don't** forget the existence check. Without it, re-running a failed loop creates duplicate webhooks.
- **Don't** hardcode secrets into the JSON heredoc that ends up in shell history — use `openssl rand -hex 32` at the top of the script and let the user pass it via env var instead.

skills.name: Global CLAUDE.md — Auto-Loaded Coding Standards
skills.description: Create ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to inject coding rules, forbidden patterns, and workflow protocols into every Claude Code session automatically — no manual pasting, no per-project setup required.
skills.body:
# Global CLAUDE.md — Auto-Loaded Coding Standards

## Problem

You have rules you want Claude Code to follow on every project — no hardcoding, no mock data, specific workflow order, security rules. But:
- You forget to paste them at session start
- Per-project CLAUDE.md gets stale or missing
- New projects start without any guardrails

## Solution

`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is loaded by Claude Code at the start of **every session, every project**, globally. Put your non-negotiable rules here once — they apply everywhere automatically.

---

## Setup

```bash
# Create the global file
touch ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
```

Then edit it with your rules. Claude Code picks it up on the next session start — no restart needed.

---

## Recommended Structure

```markdown
# Global Claude Code Rules — [Your Name]

These rules apply to EVERY project, EVERY session, automatically.

---

## ⚡ Core Workflow Protocol

[Your mandatory build order / integration protocol]

---

## 🚫 Always-Forbidden Patterns

- Never hardcode mock data in components that display live data
- Never commit .env files
- Never push directly to main
- Never use `any` in TypeScript without a comment explaining why

---

## 🔁 Default Workflow for Any New Feature

[Step-by-step order you want followed]

---

## Code Quality Rules

- try/catch on every external call (DB, API, WebSocket, LLM)
- Log failures — never swallow errors silently
- Every new function needs a 1-line comment
- No console.log in production code

---

## Project Context (global)

- Your name, timezone, active projects
- VPS SSH command, primary repos, preferred tools
```

---

## Hierarchy — Three Levels of CLAUDE.md

```
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md              ← GLOBAL: applies to every session
  ↓ merged with
<project>/.claude/CLAUDE.md     ← PROJECT: project-specific additions
  OR
<project>/CLAUDE.md             ← PROJECT: same effect, root of repo
```

Rules from all levels are merged. Project-level can add to or override global rules.

---

## What to Put in Global vs Project

| Rule Type | Global | Project |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| No hardcoding / no mock data | ✅ | |
| Security rules (.env, no main push) | ✅ | |
| Preferred workflow order | ✅ | |
| Tech stack versions | | ✅ |
| Database schema conventions | | ✅ |
| Team lead names, contacts | | ✅ |
| Project-specific API endpoints | | ✅ |

---

## Anti-Patterns to Avoid

- Don't duplicate rules between global and project — global wins, project adds
- Don't put secrets in CLAUDE.md — it may be committed to repos
- Don't make it too long — Claude Code has a context window; keep global rules under ~100 lines
- Don't mix project state (current sprint, open bugs) into global — that goes in project CLAUDE.md

---

## Example Domains

| Team | What to Put in Global CLAUDE.md |
|------|--------------------------------|
| SCADA / HMI | Zero-hardcode protocol, no mock tags, real polling only |
| Web apps | No placeholder data, Supabase key rules, branch policy |
| AI/ML | No hallucinated results in UI, always show confidence |
| Mobile | No hardcoded API URLs, environment-based config only |
| Any team | Security rules, git workflow, code quality baseline |

skills.name: Hand-Fillable PDF Blanks via Dotted-Underline CSS Spans
skills.description: When generating a PDF that will be printed and signed by hand (legal forms, KYC, lease agreements, school admission, customs declarations, vaccination certificates, MCA director-appointment forms), render every blank field as a fixed-min-width dotted-underline `<span>` — not as bracketed placeholder text like `[TO BE FILLED]`. Three CSS classes plus three small Python/JS helpers cover every case (short blank, long blank, name-or-line). The output looks professional, prints cleanly, and a person with a pen knows exactly where to write.
skills.body:
# Hand-Fillable PDF Blanks via Dotted-Underline CSS Spans ## Problem You're generating a PDF that the user will print, hand-fill, sign, and scan back. The form has a mix of: - **Pre-known values** the generator can fill (name, DOB, ID number) - **Per-filing values** that change each time (counterparty name, dates, amounts) - **Sign-on-paper values** that must remain blank (signature, hand-written initials) The naive output of most generators is awkward yellow placeholder text: > *"…Director in `[NAME OF NEW COMPANY — TO BE FILLED]` whose registered office is `[TO BE FILLED — registered office address]`…"* That looks unprofessional, photocopies poorly, and the person with the pen has to *strike through* the placeholder before writing. Worse, the eye reads "to be filled" first and misses the real prose. ## Fix — three CSS classes, three helpers ### CSS ```css .blank-line { display: inline-block; min-width: 60mm; border-bottom: 1px dotted #64748b; height: 1.1em; vertical-align: middle; } .blank-line.short { min-width: 40mm; } .blank-line.long { min-width: 100mm; } ``` That's it. A `` becomes a 60-mm dotted underline a pen can write on. Inline with the prose, no break, no awkward placeholder text. ### Renderer helpers (Python — same shape in JS) ```python def tbf(text): # short blank — single field, single line if not text or text.startswith("["): return '' return text def tbf_long(text): # long blank — addresses, sentences if not text or text.startswith("["): return '' return text def co(text): # company-name slot — bold if filled, fillable if blank if not text or text.startswith("["): return '' return f'{text}' ``` Three helpers cover ~95% of cases. The `text.startswith("[")` guard catches legacy placeholders like `[TO BE FILLED]` left over in the data file — they render as fillable lines automatically. Migration-friendly. ### Use in the template ```html

I, {{name}}, son of {{father}}, resident of {{ tbf_long(address) }}, hereby declare that I am a director of {{ co(company_name) }}, with CIN {{ tbf(cin) }}, having authorised capital of ₹ {{ tbf(authorised_capital) }}.

``` If `address` is empty, you get a 100-mm dotted line inline. If it's filled, it renders as the address. No conditional template logic, no `{% if %}` ladders. ### Table cells — even simpler For tables, just emit empty ``. The cell border itself acts as the writable box; no `` needed inside. Don't put a dotted line inside an already-bordered cell — visual clutter. ## What changes vs naive yellow placeholders | Property | Yellow `[TO BE FILLED]` | Dotted-line span | |---|---|---| | Visual noise | High — eye lands on placeholder first | Low — eye flows through prose, blanks register peripherally | | Pen workflow | Strike out placeholder, then write | Just write on the line | | Photocopy quality | Yellow background scans grey/blotchy | Dotted line scans crisply | | Form aesthetic | Looks like a draft / WIP | Looks like a finished bank form | | Migration path | Rip out every `[…]` manually | `tbf()` handles them automatically | | Print preview | Hard to spot what's blank | Blanks visible at a glance | ## Sanity-check the output Before sending the PDF to the user, grep its rendered text for leaked placeholders: ```bash for f in *.pdf; do hits=$(pdftotext "$f" - | grep -ciE 'TO BE FILLED|TO BE ALLOTTED|please confirm|format attached|placeholder') echo "$f: $hits" done ``` Any number > 0 means a `tbf()` wrap got missed somewhere. The grep catches both yellow-style placeholders and prose that escaped the helpers. ## Generic example domains | Form | Why this fits | |---|---| | Indian MCA director-appointment forms (DIR-2/8/12, MBP-1) | Many fields known per director, many vary per filing | | Lease agreement | Landlord and tenant pre-known; rent / dates / clauses fill at signing | | School admission form | Student data pre-known; signature, parent-photo blank | | Hospital admission consent | Patient pre-known; procedure, time, witness blank | | Customs declaration | Traveller pre-known; flight, hotel, items blank | | Vaccination certificate template | Patient + vaccine pre-known; dose date, batch, vaccinator blank | | Insurance proposal form | Proposer + nominee pre-known; sum-assured, payment method blank | | Tax challan template | Assessee pre-known; period, head, amount blank per filing | ## Tuning the line widths Default `min-width: 60mm` works for most short fields (names, dates, amounts in INR/USD). If a field consistently needs more or less space, add a modifier class: ```css .blank-line.tiny { min-width: 18mm; } /* a single date */ .blank-line.short { min-width: 40mm; } /* a single name */ .blank-line.long { min-width: 100mm; } /* an address */ .blank-line.full { width: 100%; } /* a paragraph */ ``` Don't overdo it — three or four widths cover everything. Past five, you're micro-managing layout that's better done by the print itself. ## Anti-patterns - **Don't** use a solid `border-bottom: 1px solid` — solid lines look like form-design from 1995. Dotted reads as "fill in the blank" universally. - **Don't** make the line height shorter than `1.1em` — descenders in handwriting (g, y, p) need room. - **Don't** colour the dotted line `#000000` — `#64748b` (slate-500) prints clean and doesn't scream from the page. - **Don't** add a placeholder ghost text inside the span (e.g. `name here`) — the user has to strike through it. Defeats the purpose. - **Don't** vary the helper signature based on field type. Three helpers is the sweet spot. More than that and the template becomes a ladder of `tbf_phone()`, `tbf_amount()`, `tbf_date()` — pointless ceremony. - **Don't** forget the `.startswith("[")` guard in `tbf()`. It's the migration trick that lets you switch a legacy template to the new pattern in one line, without auditing every call site. - **Don't** include both `display: inline-block` and `width: 100%` — one or the other. `inline-block` for inline blanks, `block` width:100% for full-line entry.
