skills.name: HTML-to-PPTX Programmatic Generation
skills.description: Generate professional PowerPoint presentations (.pptx) programmatically using python-pptx — build slides with shapes, colored cards, code blocks, flow diagrams, tables, and team cards from pure Python, no template needed.
skills.body:
# HTML-to-PPTX Programmatic Generation

## Problem

You need professional slide decks (PPTX) generated programmatically — either from existing HTML content, structured data, or from scratch. You want:
- Consistent styling across all slides
- Real `.pptx` format (editable in PowerPoint/Keynote/Google Slides)
- No dependency on a running browser or Puppeteer

## Solution

Use `python-pptx` to build slides from scratch in Python. Define reusable helper functions for common elements (cards, numbered rows, code blocks, flow steps) and call them per slide.

---

## Install

```bash
pip install python-pptx
# or on externally-managed Python (macOS Homebrew):
pip install python-pptx --break-system-packages
```

---

## Core Setup Pattern

```python
from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RGBColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN

prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width  = Inches(13.33)   # 16:9 widescreen
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

blank = prs.slide_layouts[6]       # completely blank layout
```

---

## Essential Helper Functions

```python
def add_rect(slide, x, y, w, h, fill=None, line=None):
    """Add a colored rectangle."""
    shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(1, Inches(x), Inches(y), Inches(w), Inches(h))
    shape.line.fill.background()
    if fill:
        shape.fill.solid()
        shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = fill
    else:
        shape.fill.background()
    if line:
        shape.line.color.rgb = line
        shape.line.width = Pt(1)
    else:
        shape.line.fill.background()
    return shape

def add_text(slide, text, x, y, w, h, size=18, bold=False, color=None,
             align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, wrap=True, italic=False):
    """Add a text box."""
    if color is None:
        color = RGBColor(0x1a, 0x1a, 0x2e)
    txb = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(x), Inches(y), Inches(w), Inches(h))
    txb.word_wrap = wrap
    tf = txb.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = wrap
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.alignment = align
    run = p.add_run()
    run.text = text
    run.font.size = Pt(size)
    run.font.bold = bold
    run.font.italic = italic
    run.font.color.rgb = color
    return txb

def slide_header(slide, title, subtitle="", accent=None):
    """Add a colored header bar with title and subtitle."""
    if accent is None:
        accent = RGBColor(0x0f, 0x34, 0x60)
    add_rect(slide, 0, 0, 13.33, 1.5, fill=accent)
    add_text(slide, title,    0.4, 0.18, 12.5, 0.75, size=28, bold=True,
             color=RGBColor(0xff,0xff,0xff))
    if subtitle:
        add_text(slide, subtitle, 0.4, 0.88, 12.5, 0.45, size=13,
                 color=RGBColor(0xff,0xff,0xff), italic=True)

def num_row(slide, num, text, x, y, num_color=None, size=13):
    """Numbered bullet row with colored circle."""
    if num_color is None:
        num_color = RGBColor(0xe9,0x45,0x60)
    add_rect(slide, x, y, 0.32, 0.32, fill=num_color)
    add_text(slide, str(num), x+0.04, y+0.03, 0.26, 0.28, size=10, bold=True,
             color=RGBColor(0xff,0xff,0xff), align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
    add_text(slide, text, x+0.42, y, 5.2, 0.38, size=size,
             color=RGBColor(0x37,0x41,0x51), wrap=True)

def card(slide, x, y, w, h, fill=None, border=None):
    """Rounded-looking card (rectangle with border)."""
    if fill is None:
        fill = RGBColor(0xf1,0xf5,0xf9)
    return add_rect(slide, x, y, w, h, fill=fill,
                    line=border or RGBColor(0xd1,0xd5,0xdb))

def flow_step(slide, steps_with_colors, start_x, start_y, box_w=2.2, box_h=0.45):
    """Vertical flow diagram with arrows between steps."""
    for i, (color, label) in enumerate(steps_with_colors):
        add_rect(slide, start_x, start_y + i*(box_h+0.3), box_w, box_h, fill=color)
        add_text(slide, label, start_x+0.1, start_y + i*(box_h+0.3)+0.06,
                 box_w-0.2, box_h-0.1, size=11, bold=True,
                 color=RGBColor(0xff,0xff,0xff))
        if i < len(steps_with_colors)-1:
            add_text(slide, "↓",
                     start_x + box_w/2 - 0.1,
                     start_y + i*(box_h+0.3) + box_h + 0.02,
                     0.3, 0.28, size=14,
                     color=RGBColor(0x9c,0xa3,0xaf), align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
```

---

## Slide Example — Cover Slide

```python
sl = prs.slides.add_slide(blank)
NAVY  = RGBColor(0x0f, 0x34, 0x60)
RED   = RGBColor(0xe9, 0x45, 0x60)
WHITE = RGBColor(0xff, 0xff, 0xff)

add_rect(sl, 0, 0, 13.33, 7.5, fill=NAVY)
add_rect(sl, 0, 6.8, 13.33, 0.7, fill=RED)
add_text(sl, "DAY 1 OF 7", 0.5, 0.5, 4.0, 0.4, size=11, bold=True,
         color=RGBColor(0xa8,0xd8,0xea))
add_text(sl, "Foundation Day", 0.5, 1.1, 8.0, 1.0, size=42, bold=True, color=WHITE)
add_text(sl, "Python · Git · SSH · VPS", 0.5, 2.1, 8.0, 0.5, size=16, color=WHITE)
```

---

## Slide Example — Dark Code Slide

```python
sl = prs.slides.add_slide(blank)
DARK = RGBColor(0x1e, 0x29, 0x3b)
add_rect(sl, 0, 0, 13.33, 7.5, fill=DARK)
slide_header(sl, "Git Commands Cheat Sheet", accent=RGBColor(0x0f,0x17,0x2a))

code_bg = RGBColor(0x1e, 0x29, 0x3b)
card(sl, 0.4, 2.0, 6.0, 4.5, fill=code_bg, border=RGBColor(0x33,0x41,0x55))
add_text(sl, "git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git\ngit checkout -b feature-branch",
         0.6, 2.15, 5.7, 4.2, size=11,
         color=RGBColor(0x86,0xef,0xac), wrap=False)
```

---

## Save

```python
prs.save("/path/to/output.pptx")
```

---

## Key Coordinates System

- Slide is 13.33 × 7.5 inches (16:9)
- All coordinates in `Inches(x)` from top-left corner
- Header typically occupies y=0 to y=1.5
- Content area: y=1.65 to y=6.8
- Footer/slide number: y=7.1

---

## Example Domains

| Use Case | Approach |
|----------|---------|
| Training slides | One slide per topic, helper functions for consistency |
| Weekly reports | Data-driven slides from database/CSV |
| Proposal decks | Cover + agenda + content + CTA pattern |
| Product demos | Screenshot placeholders + bullet cards |
| Intern onboarding | Day-by-day slides with code blocks + team cards |

skills.name: HTTP API Failure Isolation via Probe Matrix
skills.description: When an HTTP API call fails with an ambiguous error and you don't know whether the cause is the URL, the auth header, the request body, the model/resource name, or a billing/quota issue - run a systematic probe matrix. Define a small shell function that takes (label, url, model, headers) and curls each combination, printing the HTTP code and first N bytes of response. Identical errors across all variations means the variable being tested isn't the cause - move on. Saves hours of one-at-a-time guessing especially when provider docs are incomplete or contradictory.
skills.body:
# HTTP API Failure Isolation via Probe Matrix

## When to use

You're integrating with an HTTP API (LLM provider, payment gateway, third-party SaaS)
and getting consistent failures. The error message is vague ("authentication failed",
"insufficient balance", "model not found", "bad request"). Provider docs are
incomplete, out of date, or contradict each other. You need to know:

- Is the URL right?
- Is the auth header right?
- Is the model/resource name right?
- Is the request body shape right?
- Is it a billing/quota/permission issue at the account level?

Each variable could be the cause. Probing one at a time is slow and error-prone.

## Pattern

Write a small shell function that takes labeled parameters and curls each combination,
printing the HTTP code + the first 200-400 bytes of the response body. Run a matrix
of variations in one block. Compare outcomes side by side.

```bash
KEY="$YOUR_API_KEY"

probe() {
  local label="$1" url="$2" model="$3" header="$4"
  local code
  code="$(curl -s -o /tmp/probe.out -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 15 \
    -H "$header" \
    -H "content-type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"model\":\"$model\",\"max_tokens\":20,\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hi\"}]}" \
    "$url")"
  printf "[%-20s] %s  model=%s  http=%s\n" "$label" "$url" "$model" "$code"
  head -c 300 /tmp/probe.out; echo; echo "---"
}

# Vary URL
probe "url-A"  "https://api.example.com/v1/chat" "model-x" "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
probe "url-B"  "https://api.example.com/v2/chat" "model-x" "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"

# Vary model name
probe "model-X" "https://api.example.com/v1/chat" "model-x" "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
probe "model-Y" "https://api.example.com/v1/chat" "model-y" "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"

# Vary auth header style
probe "bearer"  "https://api.example.com/v1/chat" "model-x" "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
probe "x-api"   "https://api.example.com/v1/chat" "model-x" "x-api-key: $KEY"
```

## How to read the matrix

| Pattern | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| Identical error code + body across all rows | The variable you're testing isn't the cause. The error is upstream of every variation. |
| 404 for some URLs, working for others | URL is the issue - you found the right path. |
| 401 across all auth styles, 200 for none | The key itself is invalid (or wrong tier). Regenerate. |
| 200 for one model, "model not found" for others | Model name is the issue - you found the right one. |
| Same error code but different request_id per call | Provider IS reaching different code paths even if the user-facing error is the same - request_id helps support trace. |

## Why this beats one-at-a-time

- **Speed.** 5-10 probes in 30 seconds vs 5-10 round-trips with the user testing each.
- **Completeness.** You see all the failure modes at once, not just the first one.
- **Hypothesis killing.** When 8 variations all return identical errors, you know with certainty the cause is something none of those variations touched. That's faster than confirming each negative individually.
- **Reproducibility.** The probe block can be re-run after each fix to verify nothing else broke.

## Diagnostic vocabulary

When reporting findings, distinguish:

- **"Model X 200, Model Y 404"** - one variable's value is wrong
- **"All models 429 with code 1113"** - the variable isn't the cause; look for billing / account / endpoint-level issue
- **"All variations 200 except Model Z"** - Model Z is gated (tier, region, deprecation)
- **"All 401, regardless of header style"** - key invalid or revoked

## Saving the probes

Once you've isolated the working combination, document it next to the failed ones in
the project README or a debug log. The matrix becomes a regression-test input for
when the API changes again.

## Sensitive data hygiene

- Always source the API key from an env var, never hardcode in the probe block.
- Pipe response bodies to `head -c` so the full key (if echoed back by the server)
  doesn't fill the terminal.
- Don't paste full probe output into public chat / GitHub issues without redacting
  request_ids (they can sometimes correlate to account identifiers).

## Example Domains

| Domain | What you vary |
|--------|---------------|
| LLM provider integration (Z.AI, OpenAI proxies, custom Anthropic-compat shims) | URL × model × auth header style × body shape |
| Webhook signature debugging (Stripe, GitHub) | Header name × signing algorithm × payload encoding |
| OAuth token endpoint (Google, Microsoft, Auth0) | grant_type × scope × client_secret_post vs basic |
| Cloud SDK authentication (AWS, GCP, Azure) | profile × region × IAM role chain |
| Container registry pull (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR) | registry URL × image tag × credential helper |

## Anti-patterns

- Probing one variable at a time over multiple back-and-forth messages with the user. Slower and less informative.
- Believing the provider's first error message - it often points at a downstream symptom, not the actual cause.
- Skipping the matrix because "the docs say X" - the docs are often wrong; probe to confirm.
- Probing with a leaked key in commit history - always source from env.
- Pasting full probe output (including secrets in echoed responses) to chat or PRs without redacting.

skills.name: human-in-loop-classification-via-markdown-review
skills.description: When an AI classifier auto-files records (meetings, emails, photos, etc.) into folders but quality matters, generate a single MARKDOWN REVIEW file with one editable code block per record. User edits folder names in place, then a separate apply script reads decisions and writes files. Beats interactive prompts for batches of 30+ records.
skills.body:
# Human-in-the-Loop Classification via Markdown Review File

## Problem
You have N records (meeting summaries, photos, emails, lab samples) that an AI classifier wants to file into folders/categories. Auto-filing is fast but wrong ~10-30% of the time. Interactive `y/n` prompts in a terminal are slow and lose context. A web UI is overkill for an internal tool you'll use a few times.

**Solution: emit a single markdown review file. User edits in their editor at their own pace. A separate apply script reads decisions and acts.**

## When this pattern shines
- Classifying 20-500 records per batch
- The user is technical enough to edit a markdown file
- Records have rich context (summaries, attendees, metadata) that benefits from being seen all at once
- Wrong filings are costly to undo (e.g. data moves to public folders, gets ingested, etc.)

## Example Domains
| Domain | Records | Categories |
|---|---|---|
| Meeting capture | Fathom/Zoom transcripts | Project folders |
| Photo organizer | Camera roll | Date / event folders |
| Email triage | Inbox | Label / project / archive |
| Bug triage | New issues | Component owner / priority |
| Document filing | Scanned PDFs | Department / case number |

## File format
The review file has THREE-PART structure per record:

1. **Heading** with index + display info
2. **Editable code block** with `id:` (immutable) and `folder:` (user edits) + any other fields you want them to edit
3. **Read-only context** below (summary, attendees, AI's suggestion, confidence, reason)

```markdown
# Batch Review — Edit Then Apply

**Instructions:**
1. For each record, edit ONLY the `folder:` line inside the ```...``` code block.
2. Set to existing folder name, OR new folder (will be created), OR `SKIP` to discard.
3. Save the file. Run: `npm run batch:apply`

**Existing folders:** `Adamrit | Sales | HR | Engineering | Marketing`

---

## [1/41] 2026-05-16 — Bajaj Energy Preparatory Meeting
```
id: 147013100
folder: Sales
description: Strategy session for Bajaj Energy AI pitch — five power plants, ModAE leads
```
- attendees: Biji, Saikat, Siddharth
- suggested: **Sales** (confidence 0.95) — _explicit power plant client opportunity_
- summary excerpt: Finalize strategy for last-minute Bajaj Energy AI pitch...

---

## [2/41] 2026-05-16 — Random Impromptu Call
```
id: 147010899
folder: SKIP
description: Two-minute hello call, no business content
```
...
```

## Why code blocks for editable fields
Code blocks (` ```...``` `) survive markdown auto-formatting (Prettier, Obsidian, etc.) and look visually different from prose, signaling to the user "edit only here".

## Generator script (pseudocode)
```js
for (const record of records) {
  const cls = await classify(record);  // AI gives folder + confidence + reason
  blocks.push(`
## [${i+1}/${records.length}] ${record.title}
\`\`\`
id: ${record.id}
folder: ${cls.folder}
description: ${cls.description ?? ''}
\`\`\`
- suggested: **${cls.folder}** (confidence ${cls.confidence})
- summary: ${record.summary.slice(0, 280)}...
`);
}
writeFile('REVIEW.md', header + blocks.join('\n---\n\n'));
```

## Apply script (pseudocode)
```js
const reviewText = readFile('REVIEW.md');
const codeBlockRegex = /```\n([\s\S]*?)\n```/g;
const decisions = [];
for (const match of reviewText.matchAll(codeBlockRegex)) {
  const block = match[1];
  const id = block.match(/id:\s*(\d+)/)?.[1];
  const folder = block.match(/folder:\s*(.+)/)?.[1]?.trim();
  if (id && folder) decisions.push({ id, folder });
}
for (const d of decisions) {
  if (d.folder.toUpperCase() === 'SKIP') continue;
  const record = recordById[d.id];
  writeFile(`${d.folder}/${record.filename}`, record.content);
}
```

## Anti-patterns to avoid
- **Don't make the entire frontmatter editable.** Use one code block per record with ONLY the fields user should edit. Other context goes as prose around the block — read-only by convention.
- **Don't put `folder:` on the heading line.** Markdown formatters reshape headings; code blocks are preserved verbatim.
- **Don't regenerate REVIEW.md after user has started editing.** Once generated, treat it as the user's working file. If new records come in, append; never replace.
- **Don't fall back to `_inbox` silently when folder is unrecognized.** Print a clear warning so user knows they typo'd a folder name.

## Variants
- **Reverse decisions:** Add a `revoke:` field. Apply script can move files back.
- **Bulk override:** A `default-folder: X` line at the top sets the default for any `folder:` line left blank.
- **Multi-field editing:** Same pattern with `tags:`, `priority:`, `assignee:` lines in the code block.

## When NOT to use
- Records arrive one at a time (use interactive Slack/email approval instead)
- Non-technical users (build a real form)
- Decisions are reversible and cheap (just auto-file and let users move things later)

skills.name: Idempotent ~/.zshrc / ~/.bashrc Block Append with Marker-Based Dedupe
skills.description: Append a multi-line block of exports/aliases/path edits to a user's shell rc file via an installer that is safe to re-run. Uses a marker comment to identify the block, an awk one-liner to delete the prior block before appending, and a timestamped backup. Prevents duplicate exports from accumulating when a setup script is run multiple times.
skills.body:
# Idempotent Shell-rc Block with Marker-Based Dedupe

## Problem

A setup/install script needs to add a multi-line block (env exports, PATH edits, aliases,
shell-completion source lines) to the user's `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`. Naive
implementations:

```bash
# WRONG - appends every time the user re-runs
cat >> ~/.zshrc <<EOF
export FOO=bar
export BAZ=qux
EOF
```

After three runs the user has three identical blocks. The first one wins on shell start,
masking later changes; the user thinks the installer is broken.

`grep -q "export FOO" || cat >>` doesn't help when only one of the lines changed - you
end up with two blocks anyway.

## Pattern

Wrap the block with a unique marker comment, then on every run:

1. If the marker exists, delete the entire prior block via `awk` (marker line through next blank line)
2. Take a timestamped backup before mutating
3. Append the fresh block

```bash
SHELL_RC="${HOME}/.zshrc"
MARKER="# my-installer-name"

# Switch to ~/.bashrc for bash users
if [ -n "${BASH_VERSION:-}" ] && [ -z "${ZSH_VERSION:-}" ]; then
  SHELL_RC="${HOME}/.bashrc"
fi
[ -f "$SHELL_RC" ] || touch "$SHELL_RC"

# Dedupe guard: if marker present, strip the prior block.
if grep -Fq "$MARKER" "$SHELL_RC"; then
  BACKUP="${SHELL_RC}.bak.$(date +%s)"
  cp "$SHELL_RC" "$BACKUP"
  awk -v m="$MARKER" '
    $0 ~ m { skip=1 }
    skip && /^$/ { skip=0; next }
    !skip { print }
  ' "$BACKUP" > "$SHELL_RC"
fi

# Append fresh block. The trailing blank line is the awk delimiter for next dedupe.
cat >> "$SHELL_RC" <<EOF

$MARKER (added $(date +%Y-%m-%d))
export FOO=bar
export BAZ=qux

EOF
```

## How the awk works

```
$0 ~ m            # this line contains the marker
  { skip=1 }      # start skipping

skip && /^$/      # we are skipping AND the line is blank
  { skip=0; next} # stop skipping but drop this blank line too

!skip { print }   # otherwise print the line through to output
```

The block boundary is `marker line ... first blank line`. That blank line is consumed
so the file doesn't grow extra blank lines on re-runs.

## Why a trailing blank line in the heredoc

The dedupe relies on a blank line as the closing boundary. If your heredoc doesn't end
with one (or with two newlines before `EOF`), the next run's awk won't know where to
stop and will eat content that came after your block.

The safe heredoc pattern:

```bash
cat >> "$SHELL_RC" <<EOF

$MARKER (added $(date +%Y-%m-%d))
... your lines ...

EOF
```

Note the leading blank line (separator from prior content) and the trailing blank line
(boundary marker for next dedupe).

## Why timestamped backup

Users sometimes hand-edit their rc file inside the marker block (extra `export PATH=`
line, custom alias). The dedupe will silently delete those edits. The
`${SHELL_RC}.bak.$(date +%s)` backup gives them a recovery path. Telling them
"backed up to X" in script output makes the trade explicit.

## What this does NOT solve

- **PATH ordering** - if your block sets `PATH`, position relative to other rc lines
  matters. Re-appending always lands at the bottom.
- **Conditional sourcing** - if your block must run only inside an interactive shell or
  only on a specific OS, wrap the contents in an `if` inside the block. The dedupe
  pattern doesn't care what's in the block.
- **Other shells** - fish, nushell, and Windows PowerShell have different rc semantics.
  The marker pattern transfers but the file paths and shell builtins differ.

## Example Domains

| Domain | What goes in the block | Notes |
|--------|------------------------|-------|
| LLM provider env-vars (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek) | 3-5 `export` lines | Re-running rotates the API key without leftover ghosts |
| Cloud CLI shell completions (gcloud, aws, kubectl) | `source /path/completion.sh` | Reinstall doesn't double-source |
| Custom PATH additions (`~/.local/bin`, language version managers) | `export PATH="$HOME/.foo/bin:$PATH"` | Watch ordering caveat above |
| Project-local env (loaded only when entering dir via direnv) | use `.envrc` instead - direnv handles dedupe | Different mechanism, same goal |
| Aliases packs for a tool's interactive shell | `alias g='git'`, `alias k='kubectl'` | Backup is essential - users edit aliases |

## Anti-patterns

- `echo "export FOO=bar" >> ~/.zshrc` with no marker - duplicates on re-run.
- `sed -i` with regex over a multi-line block - sed line-mode breaks on multi-line context.
- Replacing the entire rc file - destroys user's other content.
- No backup - one bug in your awk wipes the user's customizations silently.
- No trailing blank line in the heredoc - dedupe boundary breaks, eats next run's content.
- Hardcoding `~/.zshrc` for bash users - your block lands somewhere their shell doesn't read.

skills.name: ipd-billing-flow
skills.body:
# IPD Billing Flow — Adamrit Hospital App

## When to use
Use when building, debugging, or extending anything related to bill creation, bill editing, corporate bill submission, payment collection, or bill locking in the Adamrit app.

---

## Bill Types

| Type | Page | Table | Purpose |
|------|------|-------|---------|
| **Final Bill** | `FinalBill.tsx` | `bills`, `bill_sections`, `bill_line_items` | Complete hospital bill for patient |
| **Discharge Invoice** | `DischargeInvoice.tsx` | (calculated from 8 service tables) | Auto-summed invoice at discharge |
| **Corporate Bill Submission** | `BillSubmission.tsx` | `bill_preparation` | Insurance/corporate payment tracking |
| **Gate Pass** | `GatePassModal.tsx` | `gate_passes` | Patient exit authorization |

---

## Bill Status Flow (bill_preparation table)

```
Pending Submission → Submitted → Payment Expected → Payment Received
                                                  ↘ Deduction/Dispute
```

**Status is calculated dynamically — not stored as a field:**
- `deduction_amount > 0` → `deduction_dispute` (TRUMPS all others)
- `received_amount > 0` → `payment_received`
- `expected_payment_date` set → `payment_expected`
- `date_of_submission` set → `submitted`
- None of the above → `pending_submission`

**Bill number format:** `{CORPORATE_PREFIX}-{MONTH_ABBR}-{SERIAL_NO_PADDED}`
Example: `PM-JAY-JUN-001`, `CGHS-MAY-042`
Sorted by `admission_date`, not creation date.

---

## Final Bill Sections

The final bill (`FinalBill.tsx`) is divided into sections stored in `bill_sections`:

1. **Conservative Treatment** — requires date range (date_from / date_to)
2. **Surgical Package** — requires date range
3. **Consultation** — doctor consultation charges
4. **Accommodation** — room/bed charges
5. **Pathology** — lab charges
6. **Medicine** — pharmacy
7. **Other Charges**
8. **Miscellaneous**

Each section contains line items (`bill_line_items`):
- `item_description`, `cghs_nabh_rate`, `qty`, `amount`, `item_type`, `item_order`

---

## Data Required to Create a Bill

**Patient/Visit fields:**
- Name, Age, Sex, Contact, Address
- Beneficiary Name & Relation
- Registration/IP Number
- Service Number (ECHS/CGHS)
- Category: GENERAL | OBC | SC | ST | ESIC | CGHS | ECHS
- Diagnosis, Claim ID
- Admission date, Discharge date, Bill date

**Line item fields:**
- `item_description` (required)
- `cghs_nabh_rate` — blocked for implants if missing
- `qty` — defaults to 1
- `item_type`: Standard or Surgical
- `item_order` — controls display order

**Validations:**
- Implants blocked if rate is missing
- Date ranges required for conservative treatment and surgical package sections
- Radiology items auto-merged by description to prevent duplicates

---

## Discharge Invoice Auto-Calculation

`DischargeInvoice.tsx` sums from 8 service transaction tables — NOT from the `bills` table:

| Table | Content |
|-------|---------|
| `visit_labs` | Lab charges |
| `visit_radiology` | Radiology charges |
| `visit_medications` | Pharmacy charges |
| `visit_clinical_services` | Doctor consultation charges |
| `visit_mandatory_services` | Mandatory facility charges |
| `visit_accommodations` | Room/bed charges |
| `advance_payment` | Patient advance payments (subtracted) |
| `financial_summary` | Discount totals (subtracted) |

Hidden lab items (`is_hidden = true`) are excluded.

---

## The Bill Lock Mechanism

**Location:** `FinalBill.tsx` ~line 14430

```typescript
const handlePrint = () => {
  if (isBillSubmitted || isAmountReceived) {
    toast.error('Print is locked after bill submission. Contact superadmin to unlock.');
    return;
  }
  // print logic
}
```

**Lock trigger:** `date_of_submission` set OR `received_amount > 0` in `bill_preparation`
**What is locked:** Printing the final bill
**Unlock:** Manual superadmin intervention only — no UI unlock button exists
**Rule:** Never submit/set payment before final printing is confirmed

---

## Corporate Bill Kanban (BillSubmission.tsx)

**Features:**
- Drag-and-drop between status columns (forward direction only)
- Quick amount update on Payment Received column
- Overdue tracking: 3+ days post-discharge without submission = flagged
- Corporate name badges: PM-JAY, MJPJAY, CGHS, ECHS, etc.
- Bill number auto-generated on move to Submitted column

**bill_preparation upsert rules:**
- Unique constraint on `visit_id` (one record per visit)
- Never overwrites existing field with null
- Only updates fields explicitly provided

---

## Payment Collection (Tablet)

**Module:** `src/tablet/modules/billing/BillingFlow.tsx`
**Table:** `advance_payment`
**Payment modes:** CASH, CARD, UPI, CHEQUE, NEFT

Note: `visit_id` in `advance_payment` is TEXT (visit code string), `patient_id` is UUID.

---

## Automated Billing Tasks (by shift)

From `src/components/task-optimizer/billingTasks.ts`:

| Task | Shift |
|------|-------|
| Last Night Admission Verify | Night |
| Corporate Doc Collection | Morning |
| Dialysis Morning Verify | Morning |
| Corporate Intimation | Morning |
| **Discharge Billing** | Day |
| Yojana Preauth | Morning |
| Mail Check | Day |
| Conservative Extension | Day |
| Daily Dialysis Billing | Day |
| **IPD Billing** | Day |
| NMI Query Follow-up | Evening |

---

## Key File Map

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `src/pages/FinalBill.tsx` | Main bill creation UI |
| `src/pages/EditFinalBill.tsx` | Simplified bill edit |
| `src/pages/BillSubmission.tsx` | Corporate bill Kanban |
| `src/pages/DischargeInvoice.tsx` | Auto-summed discharge invoice |
| `src/pages/ViewBill.tsx` | Read-only bill view |
| `src/components/bill-workflow/types.ts` | Status types and status logic |
| `src/components/bill-workflow/BillWorkflowCard.tsx` | Kanban card UI |
| `src/hooks/useBillSubmissions.ts` | bill_preparation CRUD + numbering |
| `src/hooks/useFinalBillData.ts` | bills/sections/line-items fetch+save |

---

## Gotchas

1. **Bill lock is permanent** — no UI unlock, superadmin only. Don't set submission date before printing.
2. **Bill line items have no uniqueness constraint** — duplicates are possible. Radiology auto-merges by description.
3. **bill_preparation upsert never nullifies existing values** — only explicit fields are updated.
4. **Discharge Invoice ≠ Final Bill** — invoice is live-calculated from service tables; final bill is a saved snapshot.
5. **Bill numbers sort by admission_date** — adding a new bill mid-month may shift serial numbers.
6. **Payment is recorded via advance_payment** — not directly on the bill record.

skills.name: ipd-discharge-summary-prompt
skills.body:
# IPD Discharge Summary — AI Prompt (Comprehensive)

## When to use
Use this prompt whenever generating an AI discharge summary in the Adamrit hospital app (`IpdDischargeSummary.tsx`). This is the canonical prompt — it replaces all previous shorter prompts.

## The Prompt (system prompt — hardcoded wrapper)

```
You are a senior medical specialist writing a comprehensive hospital discharge summary for another treating physician. Follow the template and patient data below precisely.

Non-negotiable rules:
- Do NOT include patient name, sex, or age anywhere in the document.
- Minimum 800 words for the full document.
- Use only Indian brand names for all medications.
- If surgery was performed, include detailed Operative Notes (minimum 6 sentences).
- End the document with this exact line, unchanged: URGENT CARE/ EMERGENCY CARE IS AVAILABLE 24 X 7. PLEASE CONTACT:-7030974619, 9373111709.
```

## The Prompt (OT Notes template — user-facing / stored in ot_notes_templates table)

```
You are a senior medical specialist writing a comprehensive hospital discharge summary for a doctor reader.

DOCUMENT STRUCTURE — follow this exact order:
1. **DIAGNOSIS** — primary diagnosis first, then secondary diagnoses
2. **DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS** — full table immediately after diagnosis (columns: Name [Indian brand] | Strength | Route | Dosage [English line + Hindi line] | Days)
3. Full clinical narrative — minimum 800 words, all sections below
4. **DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS** — same table repeated at the end for convenience
5. Emergency contact line (exact wording, last line)

CONTENT INSTRUCTIONS:
- For any clinical detail NOT explicitly provided in the input, invent medically plausible and specific values consistent with the diagnosis: exact vitals with numbers, specific examination findings, CBC/LFT/RFT/electrolyte values with numbers, imaging findings, events during the hospital stay, etc.
- All invented details must be internally consistent and medically appropriate for the given diagnosis.
- Do NOT add comorbidities beyond what is mentioned in the input.
- Use formal medical language throughout — this document is read by a doctor.
- Use bold headings, sub-headings, and bullet points throughout.

SECTIONS TO INCLUDE:
- **Chief Complaints** (with duration)
- **History of Present Illness** (detailed narrative)
- **Past History / Family History / Social History**
- **Clinical Examination**
  - General Examination (with specific vitals: BP, PR, RR, Temp, SpO2, weight)
  - Systemic Examination (per-system findings relevant to diagnosis)
- **Investigations**
  - Laboratory (CBC, LFT, RFT, electrolytes, coagulation — with specific numbers)
  - Radiology / Imaging (with specific findings)
  - Special Investigations (if relevant)
- **Hospital Course** (day-by-day or event-by-event narrative of admission, treatment given, clinical response, any complications during stay)
- **Operative Notes** — include ONLY if a surgery/procedure was performed:
  - Minimum 6 sentences
  - Cover: pre-operative preparation, anaesthesia type and agents, surgical approach, step-by-step operative steps, intraoperative findings, implants/mesh/sutures used, closure technique, post-operative transfer and immediate recovery
- **Condition at Discharge**
- **Discharge Advice & Home Precautions** (detailed bullet points: diet, activity, wound care, follow-up dates)
- **Warning Signs — Return to Hospital Immediately If:**
  - List ALL symptoms and signs of potential complications of the surgery performed or medical treatment received
  - Be specific (e.g. fever >101°F, wound discharge, swelling, redness, shortness of breath, etc.)

MEDICATION TABLE FORMAT:
- Use Indian brand names (Pan-D, Augmentin 625, Calpol 500, Metrogyl 400, Ceftum 500, Ecosprin 75, Atorva 10, Cremaffin Plus, etc.)
- Include 5–8 medications appropriate for the diagnosis
- Each row in Dosage column: English instruction on line 1, Hindi translation on line 2
  Example: "1 tablet twice daily after meals / एक गोली दिन में दो बार खाने के बाद"

LAST LINE (exact, do not modify):
URGENT CARE/ EMERGENCY CARE IS AVAILABLE 24 X 7. PLEASE CONTACT:-7030974619, 9373111709.
```

## Code location
- File: `src/pages/IpdDischargeSummary.tsx`
- `defaultTemplateContent` — line ~289 (fallback when DB has no templates)
- `systemPrompt` — line ~4815 (hardcoded safety wrapper sent to Gemini)
- `ot_notes_templates` Supabase table — stores the user-editable template

## Notes
- Temperature: use 0.4 for all cases (creative but medically grounded)
- Conservative vs surgical distinction is handled by the template itself ("include Operative Notes ONLY if surgery was performed")
- Patient data is auto-appended to the template: DIAGNOSIS, CLINICAL HISTORY, EXAMINATION, HOSPITAL STAY NOTES, MEDICATIONS ON DISCHARGE, ADVICE

skills.name: karpathy-guidelines
skills.description: Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring code to avoid overcomplication, make surgical changes, surface assumptions, and define verifiable success criteria.
skills.body:
# Karpathy Guidelines

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes, derived from [Andrej Karpathy's observations](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876) on LLM coding pitfalls.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

skills.name: LLM Chat Context — History Depth and Temperature Config
skills.description: Configure conversation history depth (maxHistoryMessages) and temperature on a deployed LLM chatbot to prevent context amnesia and hallucination drift. Covers OpenClaw, LangChain, and raw API patterns.
skills.body:
# LLM Chat Context — History Depth and Temperature Config

## Problem

A deployed chatbot exhibits two common symptoms:
1. **Context amnesia** — every reply feels like the bot is meeting the user for the first time; it doesn't remember what was said 2 messages ago
2. **Hallucination drift** — responses feel creative, disconnected, or make up facts; especially bad with higher temperatures (>0.8)

Both are configuration problems, not model problems.

---

## Root Causes

| Symptom | Root Cause |
|---------|------------|
| "Restarting" every message | No conversation history passed to LLM; each call is stateless |
| Weird, ungrounded replies | Temperature too high (>0.8) for a factual assistant |
| Slow, repetitive responses | Too much history (>20 messages) passed on every call |
| Ignores recent context | History not sorted by recency; oldest messages weighted too high |

---

## Fix 1 — Set History Depth

### OpenClaw (openclaw.json)

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "maxHistoryMessages": 12
    }
  }
}
```

**Rule of thumb:**
- `8–12` for WhatsApp/Telegram bots — fast, focused
- `15–20` for support/research bots — more context needed
- Never exceed `25` unless context window is very large (>100k tokens)

### LangChain / LlamaIndex

```python
from langchain.memory import ConversationBufferWindowMemory

memory = ConversationBufferWindowMemory(
    k=12,                    # keep last 12 exchanges
    return_messages=True,
    memory_key="chat_history"
)
```

### Raw API (messages[] pattern)

```python
def build_messages(history: list, new_message: str, system: str) -> list:
    """Keep last N exchanges + current message."""
    MAX_HISTORY = 12
    recent = history[-MAX_HISTORY:]   # slice to last N
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system}]
    messages.extend(recent)
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": new_message})
    return messages
```

---

## Fix 2 — Set Temperature

### Recommended Values by Use Case

| Use Case | Temperature | Reasoning |
|----------|-------------|-----------|
| WhatsApp personal assistant | 0.5–0.6 | Grounded, direct, no hallucination |
| Customer support bot | 0.3–0.5 | Accurate, consistent responses |
| Creative writing assistant | 0.7–0.9 | Varied, expressive |
| Code generation | 0.1–0.3 | Deterministic, correct |
| General conversational bot | 0.6–0.7 | Sweet spot: natural but grounded |

### OpenClaw (openclaw.json) — Two places to set it

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "temperature": 0.6
    }
  },
  "models": {
    "providers": {
      "zai": {
        "models": [
          {
            "id": "glm-4-plus",
            "temperature": 0.6
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Raw API

```python
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=messages,
    temperature=0.6,
    max_tokens=512
)
```

---

## Fix 3 — System Prompt Context Awareness Rule

Even with history configured, add an explicit instruction to the system prompt so the model *uses* the history:

```markdown
## Conversation Context Rule

Always read the last 10–15 messages from this sender before replying.
- Reference prior context — never restart cold
- If a topic was already addressed, don't repeat; just confirm or update
- Track conversation state: is this a new request or a continuation?
- If you know the user's name, role, or preferences from history — use them
```

---

## Verification — Check It's Working

After deploying: send 3–4 messages in sequence, then ask "what did I just tell you?". The bot should accurately summarise the recent exchange. If it can't, history is not being passed.

```bash
# OpenClaw: check logs to see context size per call
journalctl _PID=$(pgrep openclaw-gateway) --no-pager | grep -i "token\|context\|history" | tail -20
```

---

## Example Domains

| Platform | Where to Set |
|----------|-------------|
| OpenClaw | `openclaw.json` agents.defaults + models.providers |
| LangChain | ConversationBufferWindowMemory(k=12) |
| LlamaIndex | ChatMemoryBuffer(token_limit=4000) |
| Raw OpenAI/Anthropic | Slice messages[] array before each API call |
| Rasa / Botpress | Tracker store slot history depth |

skills.name: LLM Provider baseUrl + API-Type URL Construction Bug
skills.description: When a custom LLM provider's baseUrl already includes a version suffix and the gateway appends /v1/messages, you get /{version}/v1/messages → 404. Diagnose from the path in the error, not the HTTP status.
skills.body:
# Skill: LLM Provider baseUrl + API-Type URL Construction Bug

## Problem Pattern

A custom LLM provider is configured in a gateway (OpenClaw, LiteLLM, etc.) with:
- A `baseUrl` that ends with a version suffix like `/v4`
- An `api` type that auto-appends its own path segment like `anthropic-messages` → `/v1/messages`

Result: the gateway constructs `{baseUrl}/v1/messages` → `https://provider.com/api/paas/v4/v1/messages` → **404 Not Found**.

The 404 error body looks like:
```json
{"timestamp":"...","status":404,"error":"Not Found","path":"/v4/v1/messages"}
```

The key diagnostic signal is `/v4/v1/messages` in the path — two version segments stacked.

---

## Root Cause

Each `api` type appends a fixed path:

| api type | appended path |
|----------|--------------|
| `anthropic-messages` | `/v1/messages` |
| `openai-completions` | `/v1/chat/completions` |
| `openai-responses` | `/v1/responses` |

If `baseUrl` already ends with `/v4`, the final URL becomes:
```
https://provider.com/path/v4/v1/messages   ← WRONG (404)
```

Correct `baseUrl` should end at the path root, letting the api-type append the version:
```
https://provider.com/path                   ← RIGHT
→ https://provider.com/path/v1/messages
```

---

## Diagnosis Checklist

When a WhatsApp/Telegram bot stops replying with 404 errors:

1. **Read the path in the 404** — `/v4/v1/messages` means double-version stacking
2. **Find the provider config** — check `models.json` or `openclaw.json` → `models.providers`
3. **Check `baseUrl` for a trailing version** — `/v4`, `/v3`, `/v2` at the end is the bug
4. **Check `api` type** — `anthropic-messages` or `openai-completions` both auto-append
5. **Decide**: strip trailing version from baseUrl, OR switch to a working provider

---

## Quick Recovery When Bot Stops Responding

### Step 1: See what's configured and has auth

```bash
openclaw models list   # on the gateway host
```

Output shows `Auth: yes/no` per model. Only switch to models with `Auth: yes`.

```
Model                        Input    Ctx    Local Auth  Tags
zai/glm-4-plus               text     195k   no    yes   default
openrouter/z-ai/glm-5.1      text     198k   no    yes   configured
openai/gpt-4o-mini            text     128k   no    yes   configured
```

### Step 2: Find real API keys (TWO places to check)

OpenClaw has API keys in **two separate places** — check both:

```bash
# Place 1: systemd/launchd service file
cat /root/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service | grep -i "_API_KEY\|_TOKEN"

# Place 2: openclaw.json env section (often overlooked!)
python3 -c "import json; d=json.load(open('/root/.openclaw/openclaw.json')); print(list(d.get('env',{}).keys()))"
```

The `openclaw.json` `env` section is read at startup and injected into the gateway process — it's a config-file alternative to systemd `Environment=` lines. Real API keys are often here even when absent from the service file.

### Step 3: Switch to a working model

```bash
# One-liner: change both default and per-agent override
ssh root@host "python3 -c \"
import json; path='/root/.openclaw/openclaw.json'; cfg=json.load(open(path))
m='openai/gpt-4o-mini'
cfg['agents']['defaults']['model']['primary']=m
[a.update({'model':m}) for a in cfg.get('agents',{}).get('list',[]) if a['id']=='main']
json.dump(cfg,open(path,'w'),indent=2)
print('switched to',m)\""
# Gateway hot-reloads agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.list
```

---

## Probe First: Detect Provider API Format with curl

Before configuring `api` type, test both formats directly. A 200 or 4xx (auth/billing) = right path. A 404 = wrong path.

```bash
# Test Anthropic-compatible format
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X POST {PROVIDER_BASE_URL}/v1/messages \
  -H 'x-api-key: YOUR_KEY' \
  -H 'anthropic-version: 2023-06-01' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"MODEL_ID","max_tokens":10,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'

# Test OpenAI-compatible format
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X POST {PROVIDER_BASE_URL}/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_KEY' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"MODEL_ID","max_tokens":10,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
```

| Response | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `200` | Correct format — use this `api` type |
| `401` / `403` | Wrong key, but correct path — use this `api` type |
| `429` + billing error | Correct path, account out of credits — use this `api` type |
| `404` | Wrong path — try the other format |

**Z.AI result (2026-04-13):** `/v4/messages` → 404, `/v4/chat/completions` → 429 (billing). Z.AI uses **OpenAI-compatible format**.

---

## Fix Options

### Option A: Wrong api type (provider uses different format than configured)

```json
// BEFORE (broken) — ZAI example: baseUrl correct, api type wrong
"zai": {
  "baseUrl": "https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4",
  "api": "anthropic-messages"   // ← appends /v1/messages → 404
}

// AFTER (fixed) — use openai-completions: appends /chat/completions → 200
"zai": {
  "baseUrl": "https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4",
  "api": "openai-completions"
}
```

### Option B: Wrong baseUrl (version suffix stacking)

```json
// BEFORE (broken) — baseUrl already has /v4, anthropic-messages adds /v1/messages
"provider": {
  "baseUrl": "https://provider.com/api/v4",
  "api": "anthropic-messages"   // → /api/v4/v1/messages (404)
}

// AFTER — strip trailing version from baseUrl
"provider": {
  "baseUrl": "https://provider.com/api",
  "api": "anthropic-messages"   // → /api/v1/messages (200)
}
```

### Option C: Switch primary model to a known-working provider (fastest fix)

```bash
# OpenClaw: edit openclaw.json agents.defaults.model.primary
python3 -c "
import json
path = '/root/.openclaw/openclaw.json'
cfg = json.load(open(path))
cfg['agents']['defaults']['model']['primary'] = 'openrouter/auto'
json.dump(cfg, open(path,'w'), indent=2)
"
# Gateway hot-reloads this field — no restart needed
```

---

## Example Domains

| Domain | Provider Example | Bad baseUrl | Good baseUrl |
|--------|-----------------|-------------|--------------|
| Z.AI (ZhipuAI) | `zai/glm-4-plus` | baseUrl correct; wrong `api` type (`anthropic-messages` → use `openai-completions`) | baseUrl `https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4` + `api: "openai-completions"` |
| Azure OpenAI | `azure/gpt-4o` | `https://myapp.openai.azure.com/openai/v1` | `https://myapp.openai.azure.com/openai` |
| Self-hosted Ollama proxy | `local/llama3` | `http://localhost:11434/api/v1` | `http://localhost:11434/api` |

---

## Hot-Reload Behaviour (OpenClaw-specific)

OpenClaw gateway watches `openclaw.json` for changes and hot-reloads certain fields including `agents.defaults.model.primary`. You will see in systemd logs:

```
[reload] config change detected; evaluating reload (agents.defaults.model.primary)
[reload] config hot reload applied (agents.defaults.model.primary)
```

No restart needed for model changes. Other config changes (channels, auth) typically require restart.

---

## Critical: Per-Agent Model Override Takes Precedence Over Default

When changing `agents.defaults.model.primary`, also check `agents.list[]` for per-agent overrides:

```json
"agents": {
  "defaults": { "model": { "primary": "openrouter/auto" } },  // ← change this
  "list": [
    { "id": "main", "model": "zai/glm-4-plus" }              // ← AND this!
  ]
}
```

The per-agent `model` field overrides the default — changing only the default while the per-agent override remains will still fail. Fix both in one python3 call:

```bash
python3 -c "
import json
path = '/root/.openclaw/openclaw.json'
cfg = json.load(open(path))
new_model = 'anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001'
cfg['agents']['defaults']['model']['primary'] = new_model
for agent in cfg.get('agents', {}).get('list', []):
    if agent.get('id') == 'main':
        agent['model'] = new_model
json.dump(cfg, open(path,'w'), indent=2)
"
# Gateway hot-reloads both fields in one pass
```

## Which Provider Actually Has Keys?

Before switching models, verify which providers have real credentials:

```bash
# Check systemd env for API keys
cat /root/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service | grep -i "_API_KEY\|_TOKEN"

# Check agent auth-profiles.json for token-based auth
cat /root/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/auth-profiles.json
```

| Provider | Where key lives | Check |
|----------|----------------|-------|
| Anthropic | `auth-profiles.json` (`token` type) | `lastGood.anthropic` present |
| OpenRouter | systemd `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` env | look in service file |
| OpenAI | systemd `OPENAI_API_KEY` env | look in service file |
| ZAI | `openclaw.json` models.providers.zai.apiKey | inline in config |

## Related

- `openclaw-whatsapp-loop-fix` — other reasons the bot stops responding
- `credential-survivorship-audit` — stale credentials surviving config changes

skills.name: Mac Disk Space Cleanup Playbook
skills.description: Systematic Mac disk space recovery — ordered by impact. Covers Chrome AI models, screen recordings, node_modules, Zoom recordings, app caches, iOS DeviceSupport, pnpm store, and Python venvs. Includes a reusable audit script.
skills.body:
# Mac Disk Space Cleanup Playbook

Ordered by typical space recovered. Run the audit first, then delete by category.

## Quick Audit

```bash
# Top-level sizes
du -d 1 ~ 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head -15

# Documents breakdown (often has huge Zoom folder)
du -d 1 ~/Documents/ 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head -10

# Library breakdown
du -d 1 ~/Library/ 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head -10

# All node_modules with sizes
find ~ -maxdepth 6 -name "node_modules" -type d \
  -not -path "*/node_modules/*/node_modules" 2>/dev/null | \
  xargs -I{} du -sh {} 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -30

# App caches breakdown
du -sh ~/Library/Caches/*/ 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20
```

## Category Cleanup (Highest Impact First)

### 1. Zoom Recordings — often 40-90 GB

```bash
du -sh ~/Documents/Zoom/
ls ~/Documents/Zoom/ | wc -l   # number of recordings
# Delete all (irreversible — export to cloud first if needed):
rm -rf ~/Documents/Zoom/
```

### 2. Chrome AI Model + Caches — 8-14 GB (see `macos-chrome-disk-write-crash-fix` skill)

```bash
# Requires Chrome to be closed
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Google/Chrome/OptGuideOnDeviceModel/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome/
```

### 3. Screen Recordings — often 10-25 GB on Desktop

```bash
du -sh ~/Desktop/*.mov 2>/dev/null | sort -rh
# Delete macOS default-named screen recordings:
rm ~/Desktop/Screen\ Recording\ *.mov
```

### 4. Screenshots — 100-500 MB, clutter

```bash
ls ~/Desktop/Screenshot*.png | wc -l
rm ~/Desktop/Screenshot*.png
rm ~/Desktop/Screenshot*.jpg 2>/dev/null
```

### 5. node_modules — 15-30 GB across projects

```bash
# Find all (exclude global npm packages)
find ~ -maxdepth 7 -name "node_modules" -type d \
  -not -path "*/.npm-global/*" \
  -not -path "*/node_modules/*/node_modules" \
  2>/dev/null > /tmp/nm_list.txt

wc -l /tmp/nm_list.txt          # count
du -ch $(cat /tmp/nm_list.txt) 2>/dev/null | tail -1  # total size

# Delete all (run npm/yarn install per project when needed):
while IFS= read -r dir; do rm -rf "$dir"; done < /tmp/nm_list.txt
```

### 6. iOS DeviceSupport Symbols — 4-10 GB

```bash
du -sh ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS\ DeviceSupport/
# Safe to delete — re-downloaded when you plug in your device:
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS\ DeviceSupport/
```

### 7. App Caches — 1-3 GB

```bash
# Safe to delete (all regenerated automatically):
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/typescript/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/pip/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/node-gyp/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/Homebrew/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/electron/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/canva-updater/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm/
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/Firefox/
```

### 8. Python venvs in backup/archive folders — 500 MB - 1 GB

```bash
# Find venvs
find ~/1backup ~ -maxdepth 5 -name "venv" -o -name ".venv" 2>/dev/null | \
  xargs du -sh 2>/dev/null | sort -rh

# Delete venvs only inside backup/archive dirs — keep active project venvs:
find ~/1backup -name "venv" -o -name ".venv" 2>/dev/null | \
  xargs rm -rf
```

### 9. .next Build Artifacts — 500 MB - 1 GB

```bash
find ~ -maxdepth 6 -name ".next" -type d 2>/dev/null | \
  xargs du -sh 2>/dev/null | sort -rh
# Delete (rebuilt with `npm run build`):
find ~ -maxdepth 6 -name ".next" -type d -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null
```

### 10. pnpm Store — prune orphaned packages

```bash
pnpm store prune
```

### 11. .DS_Store Files (clutter, not space)

```bash
find ~/Desktop ~/Downloads ~/Documents -name ".DS_Store" -delete 2>/dev/null
```

### 12. Xcode DerivedData — 0-20 GB (if doing iOS/macOS dev)

```bash
du -sh ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/
```

## Do NOT Delete

- `~/.npm-global/lib/node_modules` — globally installed CLI tools (`pm2`, `nodemon`, etc.)
- Active project `venv`/`.venv` outside backup directories
- `~/Downloads` — likely contains work documents
- Chrome profile session data (bookmarks, passwords live here)

## Space Recovery Summary (typical Mac developer)

| Category | Typical Recovery |
|----------|----------------|
| Zoom recordings | 40-90 GB |
| node_modules | 15-30 GB |
| Chrome AI model + caches | 8-14 GB |
| Screen recordings | 5-25 GB |
| iOS DeviceSupport | 4-10 GB |
| Xcode DerivedData | 2-20 GB |
| App caches | 1-3 GB |
| Screenshots + .DS_Store | <1 GB |

## Example Domains

| Context | Notes |
|---------|-------|
| macOS developer machine | Full playbook applies |
| macOS non-developer | Skip node_modules, Xcode, pnpm sections |
| macOS CI runner | Focus on caches and build artifacts |

skills.name: macOS Chrome Disk-Write Quota Crash Fix
skills.description: Diagnose and fix Chrome being killed by macOS for exceeding disk write limits — root cause is the 4 GB OptGuideOnDeviceModel AI model rewriting itself constantly. Fix via policy + cache cleanup.
skills.body:
# macOS Chrome Disk-Write Quota Crash Fix

## Symptom

Chrome crashes repeatedly with no obvious cause. The macOS diagnostic report at `/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/Google Chrome_*.diag` shows:

```
Event:            disk writes
Writes:           2147.50 MB of file backed memory dirtied over 8050 seconds
                  (266.75 KB per second average), exceeding limit of 24.86 KB per second
```

macOS enforces a rolling 24-hour disk write budget (~25 KB/s average). Chrome is terminated — not crashed — when it exceeds this quota.

## Root Causes (in order of impact)

| Culprit | Size | Why it writes so much |
|---------|------|----------------------|
| `OptGuideOnDeviceModel/` | 4 GB | Chrome's on-device AI navigation model — continuously re-trained and rewritten |
| Disk caches across 20+ profiles | 4+ GB | No size cap by default |
| Service Worker caches | 700 MB+ | Dirtied on every page load |
| `optimization_guide_model_store/` | 150 MB | Same AI pipeline |
| `SODALanguagePacks/` | 190 MB | Speech recognition data |

## Diagnosis

```bash
# Check crash type in system diagnostic reports
ls -lt /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ | grep -i chrome | head -10

# Read the crash — look for "Event: disk writes"
head -40 "/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/Google Chrome_<timestamp>.diag"

# Check profile and cache sizes
du -sh ~/Library/Application\ Support/Google/Chrome/
du -sh ~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome/

# See profile breakdown
du -sh ~/Library/Application\ Support/Google/Chrome/*/ | sort -rh | head -10
```

## Fix — Step 1: Apply Chrome Policies (takes effect on next restart)

```bash
# Cap disk cache to 256 MB (default is unlimited)
defaults write com.google.Chrome DiskCacheSize -int 268435456

# Disable on-device AI model fetching (eliminates the 4 GB write source)
defaults write com.google.Chrome OptimizationGuideFetchingEnabled -bool false

# Verify
defaults read com.google.Chrome
```

## Fix — Step 2: Run Cleanup Script (requires Chrome to be closed)

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Save as ~/chrome_cleanup.sh, chmod +x, run after quitting Chrome

if pgrep -x "Google Chrome" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ERROR: Quit Chrome first (Cmd+Q), then run this script."
  exit 1
fi

SUPPORT=~/Library/Application\ Support/Google/Chrome
CACHE=~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome

# The #1 write source — 4 GB AI model
rm -rf "$SUPPORT/OptGuideOnDeviceModel"
rm -rf "$SUPPORT/optimization_guide_model_store"

# All disk caches
rm -rf "$CACHE"

# Service Worker + Code Cache + GPU Cache in every profile
for p in "$SUPPORT"/Default "$SUPPORT"/Profile\ */; do
  rm -rf "$p/Service Worker" "$p/Code Cache" "$p/GPUCache" "$p/Shared Dictionary"
done

# Speech recognition packs
rm -rf "$SUPPORT/SODA" "$SUPPORT/SODALanguagePacks"

echo "Done. Chrome profile: $(du -sh "$SUPPORT" 2>/dev/null)"
```

## Why This Works

- `DiskCacheSize` stops Chrome from treating the disk as unlimited HTTP cache storage.
- `OptimizationGuideFetchingEnabled = false` prevents Chrome from downloading and continuously rewriting its ML model for navigation prediction. This single change eliminates the largest write source.
- Clearing existing caches removes the backlog of dirty pages already waiting to be flushed.

## Example Domains

| Context | Same Pattern |
|---------|-------------|
| Chrome on any Mac | Applies directly |
| Chromium-based browsers (Edge, Brave) | Same `defaults write` key names |
| Any app killed for `disk writes` | Check `/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/` for `Event: disk writes` |

## Recurrence Prevention

Re-run the cleanup script monthly. The policies persist across Chrome updates since they live in macOS user preferences, not inside the app bundle.

```bash
# Quick check: is Chrome over budget today?
grep "Event:" /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/Google\ Chrome_*.diag 2>/dev/null | tail -5
```

skills.name: MCA Director-Appointment Form Generator (DIR-2 / DIR-8 / MBP-1 / Info Template)

The user keeps verified KYC values in a single Python data file; weasyprint converts a styled HTML template into clean A4 PDFs with bold lock-printed values and dotted underlines wherever the field is blank for hand-fill. Solves the recurring pain of re-typing the same name/PAN/Aadhaar/DIN into many .docx templates each time a new directorship is filed.
skills.body: # MCA Director-Appointment Form Generator ## When to use this You're filing a new director appointment with India's MCA and the company secretary asks for the standard packet: - **Form DIR-2** — Consent to act as a director (§152(5) + Rule 8) - **Form DIR-8** — Intimation by Director on disqualification (§164(2) + Rule 14(1)) - **Form MBP-1** — Notice of interest by director (§184(1) + Rule 9(1)) - **Director Appointment Information Template** — covers company + personal details + documentation checklist These forms are the same fields every time, with the same legal text. Re-typing into Word `.docx` templates is wasteful. This skill scaffolds a one-file data store + an HTML→PDF generator so the second-and-onward filing takes seconds, not an evening. ## What gets generated Four A4 PDFs to the user's Desktop (or any chosen folder), with: - Locked-printed values for the parts you've verified once (name, DIN, PAN, Aadhaar, parents, DOB, address, phone, email, qualifications, occupation, place, date) - Clean dotted underlines for the parts that change per filing (new company name, CIN, registered office, capital figures, fee/salary, signature) - Tabulated existing-directorships and interest-disclosures rows that pull from a Python list — adding a new row is a one-line edit ## File layout ``` /tmp/forms-fill/ ├── _data.py # Single source of truth — KYC + company info + lists └── build.py # weasyprint generator ``` ## `_data.py` template ```python """Director appointment form data — → .""" D = { # Director (personal) — name as registered with DIN at MCA. "name": "First Middle Last", "father": "...", "mother": "...", "spouse": "...", "dob": "DD/MM/YYYY", "place_of_birth": "City, State, Country", "gender": "Male" | "Female" | "Other", "nationality": "Indian", "din": "00000000", # 8 digits, no spaces "pan": "ABCDE1234F", "aadhaar": "XXXX XXXX XXXX", # display format "passport": "X0000000", "dl": "MH00 00000000000", "mobile": "+91 9XXXXXXXXX", "email": "name@example.com", "address_full": "Full address as on Aadhaar, ending PIN", "qualification": "MBBS, MS", # any post-nominals "occupation": "...", "membership_no": "Not Applicable", # for company-secretary applicants # Company being appointed director of — leave "" for hand-fill. "co_name": "", "co_pan": "", "co_doi": "", "co_cin": "", "co_address": "", "co_nominal": "", "co_paidup": "", # Existing directorships in the last 3 years (DIR-8). "directorships": [ # (Company name with CIN, Date of appointment or "", Date of cessation or "Continuing") ("FOO PRIVATE LIMITED (CIN U00000XX0000PTC000000)", "", "Continuing"), ], # MBP-1 §184(1) interests. "interests": [ # (Name with CIN, Nature of interest, Shareholding %, Date arose) ("FOO PRIVATE LIMITED (CIN U00000XX0000PTC000000)", "Director", "80%", ""), ], "place": "City", "date": "DD/MM/YYYY", "no_of_companies": "1", "appointment_type":"Executive Director / Whole-Time Director", } ``` ## `build.py` outline The generator uses three small helpers to make blanks render as fillable lines instead of awkward placeholder text: ```python def tbf(text): # short blank if not text or text.startswith("["): return '' return text def tbf_long(text): # long blank (addresses) if not text or text.startswith("["): return '' return text def co(text): # company-name slot — bold if filled, fillable line if blank if not text or text.startswith("["): return '' return f'{text}' ``` CSS for the fillable line: ```css .blank-line { display: inline-block; min-width: 60mm; border-bottom: 1px dotted #64748b; height: 1.1em; vertical-align: middle; } .blank-line.long { min-width: 100mm; } ``` Each form is its own function returning HTML. The bottom of the file maps name→html and writes via: ```python subprocess.run(["weasyprint", "/tmp/_tmp.html", out_path], check=True) ``` ## Common pitfalls | Mistake | Fix | |---|---| | Yellow `[TO BE FILLED]` placeholder text leaks into the printed PDF | Use the `tbf/tbf_long/co` helpers everywhere a value might be blank, never inline `{D["co_name"]}`. | | Director name on PAN differs from name on DIN | Print the **DIN-registered** name in MCA-form fields. The PAN-spelling can go alongside in a comment in `_data.py` for traceability. | | User says "remove company X from the form" | Set the relevant row in `directorships` / `interests` lists to `("", "", "")` (or remove). Then update `no_of_companies`, and update DIR-2 row 11 wording in `build.py` so it doesn't hardcode the old name. | | AMBUFAST / similar — relative is the director, not the user | Exclude from `interests` (MBP-1 §184(1) is the director's *own* interests). Family-member directorships flow under §188 disclosure, not here. | | weasyprint warnings about `inset:0`, `backdrop-filter`, `stroke-width` | Cosmetic only — outputs still render correctly. Filter with `grep -v WARNING` in the build wrapper. | ## Idempotent verification After every regenerate, sanity-check the rendered text: ```bash for f in ~/Desktop/Director\ —\ *.pdf; do hits=$(pdftotext "$f" - | grep -ciE 'TO BE FILLED|please confirm|format attached') echo "$f: $hits" done ``` If any number is non-zero you missed a `tbf()` wrap somewhere. ## Example domains | Setting | What you'd customise | |---|---| | Indian Pvt Ltd incorporation | All four forms; multi-director by duplicating `_data.py` per director | | LLP partner appointment | Swap forms (Form 4 / Form 8); same generator pattern | | Adding a director to existing company | Same packet, new `co_*` values, additional row in `directorships` | | Resignation (DIR-12) | Different form template; same `_data.py` reuse | | Foreign-director onboarding | Add passport-issue/expiry as a top-level field, render in Identity section | ## Why this beats editing the .docx templates - **Single source of truth** — change name/address once in `_data.py`, all four PDFs reflect it. Editing four `.docx` files individually is where bugs sneak in. - **No LibreOffice / Word required** — pure Python + weasyprint. Works on any Mac with `pip install weasyprint`. - **Cleaner output** — typography from Inter; dotted blanks are visibly fillable; printed values are visibly locked. Reads better than the reference `.docx`s. - **Memory-friendly** — pair this skill with a project-memory file that holds the verified KYC values; the next director-appointment filing is a one-line `_data.py` edit + one `python3 build.py`.

skills.name: merge-revert-on-broken-prod
skills.description: When a feature-branch merge breaks production (UI distortion, layout regressions, broken auth, etc.), `git revert -m 1 <merge-commit>` is the right move — it cleanly undoes the merged changes, preserves history, requires no force-push, and ships through the normal CI/CD path. Use when you need to roll back a merge on a shared branch without rewriting history.
skills.body:
# Reverting a Merge Commit That Broke Production

A feature branch was merged to `main`, the CI/CD pipeline deployed it, and production immediately broke — distorted UI, missing layout, broken navigation, or worse. You need to restore the prior state **now**, without rewriting history (which would force-push and disrupt anyone else on the branch).

The correct command is `git revert -m 1 <merge-commit>`, not `git reset --hard`.

## Why `revert -m 1`, not `reset --hard`

| Option | Result | When |
|--------|--------|------|
| `git revert -m 1 <merge>` | Adds one new commit that undoes the merge. Branch advances forward. No force-push. Other engineers' clones stay valid. | **Default for a shared branch.** Always safe. |
| `git reset --hard <prev>` + force-push | Branch pointer moves backward. Erases the merge from history. Other clones get rejected on next pull. Loses the feature work from `main` (it survives only on the feature branch). | Solo branches only, or when you must rewrite history for compliance reasons. |

`-m 1` means "this is a merge with two parents; revert toward parent 1 (the mainline)." Parent 2 is the feature branch being undone.

## Identify the merge first

```bash
git log --oneline --graph -10
# Look for "Merge: aaa bbb" entries — those are merge commits.
git show --stat <merge-sha>   # Confirm files affected
```

If the breaking commit is a normal (non-merge) commit, drop `-m 1`:
```bash
git revert <normal-commit-sha>
```

## The revert + deploy + verify loop

```bash
# 1. Clean working tree (revert refuses to run with unstaged changes)
git stash push -u -m "pre-revert"

# 2. Revert the merge. --no-edit takes the default revert message.
git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> --no-edit

# 3. Confirm the revert touched the expected files
git show --stat HEAD

# 4. Push — CI/CD redeploys automatically
git push

# 5. Restore your in-progress work
git stash pop
```

Then **verify in production** — don't trust that the revert worked just because it pushed:

```bash
# Wait for the production deploy to be READY, then smoke-test:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://<prod>/<route-that-was-broken>
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://<prod>/<route-that-should-still-work>

# Bust CDN cache when probing, since edge servers may still serve the broken response:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://<prod>/<route>?cb=$(date +%s)"
```

After the deploy lands, the user must **hard-refresh** their browser (Cmd+Shift+R / Ctrl+F5) to drop their own cached HTML / JS bundles.

## To bring the feature back later

Nothing is lost. `git revert <revert-commit>` re-applies the original changes. Then fix the actual root cause (e.g., redo the Navigation rewrite incrementally instead of in one mass-rewrite).

## Database / migration caveat

`git revert` rolls back **code only**. If the reverted commit included DB migrations that already ran, those tables/columns still exist. They're usually harmless to leave (unused tables don't hurt anything), but if they conflict with the reverted code's old schema expectations, drop them explicitly via a follow-up SQL.

## Example Domains

| Stack | What you'd revert |
|-------|-------------------|
| Vercel + Next.js | A merge that rewrote `components/Navigation.tsx`, breaking the sidebar |
| Netlify + Gatsby | A merge that swapped a global layout component |
| Rails app on Heroku | A merge that changed `application.html.erb` and broke nav for all pages |
| Mobile (React Native) via CodePush / EAS | Cannot revert a binary release the same way — must publish a new build; same `git revert` pattern works for the code, the platform handles delivery |
| Internal admin tool (Django + nginx) | A merge that rewrote `base.html`; revert + `systemctl reload` to redeploy |

## Verify checklist

- [ ] Revert commit shows in `git log` (not a reset that erased history)
- [ ] Production deploy reaches READY after the push
- [ ] Routes that were broken now return their expected status
- [ ] Routes added by the reverted feature now return 404 (confirms they're gone)
- [ ] Routes unrelated to the feature still return their normal status
- [ ] You hard-refreshed the browser (CDN + browser cache both flushed)
- [ ] A memory note records what was reverted and why, so future sessions don't accidentally bring it back without fixing the original bug

skills.name: multi-agent-code-review-fanout
skills.description: Parallel code review by fanning out one Agent per file/feature surface. Each agent gets a focused per-file prompt with specific concerns and a word cap; the parent synthesizes their independent reports into a ranked punch list. Beats sequential review because each agent has clean context and the parent deduplicates findings.
skills.body:
# Multi-Agent Code Review Fan-Out

## Problem
You just finished a multi-file feature or bug-fix sweep and want a second pass before pushing. A single review pass on a long context drifts — the reviewer forgets the early findings by the time it gets to the last file, mixes concerns across files, and skips edge cases that need a fresh read.

A parallel fan-out gives you:
- One clean review context per file (no drift, no mixing).
- Truly independent findings (one agent doesn't anchor on another's).
- Faster wall-clock time than serial review.
- A parent pass that deduplicates and ranks — better than dumping raw reports on the user.

## When to use

| Use it | Skip it |
|---|---|
| 2–6 independent files/features changed | Single-file change |
| Each change has its own concerns | All changes are the same refactor |
| Files don't overlap or depend tightly | Tightly coupled changes need cross-file review |
| Pre-push gate on a multi-commit branch | Quick syntax-level review |

## Pattern

### 1. Identify discrete review surfaces

Each surface = one agent. A surface is typically one file, but could be one feature spanning a couple of small files. Aim for 3–5 surfaces; more than 6 is hard to synthesize.

### 2. Brief each agent specifically

Bad prompt (generic):
> "Review X.tsx for bugs."

Good prompt:
> "Review X.tsx. Context: recently extended with Y (specific change). Review for: (a) the drag handler operating on `items` vs the rendered `filteredItems` — index mismatch risk; (b) Promise.all error handling; (c) JSX balance after adding the drag handle wrapper. Report file:line, severity, suggested one-line fix. Under 400 words."

Each prompt should include:
- **Exact file path** (no globs)
- **Brief context** of what changed and why
- **Specific concerns** to check — the ones you already suspect
- **Output format**: file:line + severity + one-line fix
- **Word cap** (300–500 words)
- **Read-only directive**: "Do NOT write code — report findings only"

### 3. Launch in parallel, in one message

```
Agent("Review file A", subagent_type="general-purpose", prompt="...A-specific...")
Agent("Review file B", subagent_type="general-purpose", prompt="...B-specific...")
Agent("Review file C", subagent_type="general-purpose", prompt="...C-specific...")
```

All three in a single response = parallel execution.

### 4. Synthesize, don't relay

When all reports come back:
- Don't dump three blocks of text on the user.
- Deduplicate (if two agents flagged the same minor issue, merge).
- Rank by severity (HIGH first, MEDIUM, LOW).
- Add file:line refs so the user can act.
- Note when one agent disagrees with another and which seems right.

The parent's value is the synthesis. If you skip it, the user gets three disconnected reviews and has to do the deduplication themselves.

## Example prompt template

```
You are reviewing recent changes to a [STACK] project. Review ONLY this
file for bugs, edge cases, and consistency issues. Do NOT write code —
report findings only.

File: /absolute/path/to/file.ext

Context: [1-2 sentences on what this file does and what recently changed]

Review specifically for:
- [Suspected concern 1 with hint about where to look]
- [Suspected concern 2]
- [Suspected concern 3]

Report a concise punch list: each issue with file:line, severity
(high/medium/low), and a one-line suggested fix. Under 400 words.
```

## Example domains

| Domain | Surfaces |
|---|---|
| Feature branch with N modified files | one agent per file |
| Migration (DB + ORM model + UI form + tests) | one agent per layer |
| Multi-service feature | one agent per service |
| Multi-page UI change | one agent per page component |
| Refactor across modules | one agent per module |

## Anti-patterns

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| Same generic prompt to all agents | Reports become identical — you lose the parallel benefit |
| No word cap | Agents over-elaborate; context returns blow up |
| Cross-file concerns split across agents | Each agent only sees one side; no one catches the seam |
| Letting agents write code | They make uncoordinated edits; sequential single-fix path is safer |
| Forwarding raw reports to the user | User pays the synthesis cost you should pay |

## Why this beats sequential review

A single reviewer with 5 files in context will:
- Anchor on the first file's findings, framing later files in those terms.
- Forget specifics about the first file by the time it gets to the fifth.
- Mix concerns ("the bug in A is similar to B" — but it's not, you just had B's pattern in mind).

Five fresh contexts each looking at one file → cleaner findings. The parent's job is to spot when one agent missed a cross-file concern.

## Trust but verify

An agent's summary describes what it intended to check, not necessarily what it found. Before relaying a "HIGH severity" claim to the user, glance at the cited file:line yourself. Agents will sometimes confidently report a bug that's actually fine in context, or miss a real bug that was outside their prompt's stated concerns. The parent is the last filter.
