skills.name: Responsive shadcn Dialog with Pinned Header/Footer and Scrollable Body
skills.description: Make a shadcn (Radix UI) `<DialogContent>` responsive on small viewports — body content scrolls inside the dialog while the header (title) and footer (action buttons) stay pinned and always visible. Uses flex column layout with `max-h-[90vh]` and `overflow-y-auto` on a flex-1 wrapper, plus `w-[95vw]` for width responsiveness.
skills.body:
# Responsive shadcn Dialog with Pinned Header/Footer ## Symptom A shadcn/Radix `` with a long form pushes the Save/Cancel buttons off the bottom of the viewport. On smaller screens (1280×800 laptops, tablets), users scroll the page to reach the buttons or hit `Esc` to cancel — which closes the dialog and loses their input. ```tsx Edit Item
{/* …many form fields, total height ≈ 1200px… */}
{/* ← off-screen on a 768px-tall viewport */} ``` ## The fix Convert `` to a constrained **flex column**, make the body the only flex child that grows + scrolls, and pin the header + footer with `shrink-0`. ```tsx Edit Item {/* Scrollable body — flex-1 grows to fill, overflow-y-auto scrolls */}
{/* …form fields… */}
``` ## Why each class matters | Class | What it does | |-------|--------------| | `w-[95vw]` | Dialog scales with viewport width — never wider than 95% of screen | | `max-w-2xl` | Caps the width on desktop so it doesn't sprawl | | `max-h-[90vh]` | Caps the height — without this, content height drives total dialog height | | `flex flex-col` | Makes header / body / footer stack as flex items | | `p-0` | Removes default padding so children can manage their own padding | | `shrink-0` (header + footer) | Prevents header/footer from shrinking when body content is tall | | `flex-1` (body) | Body takes all remaining vertical space | | `overflow-y-auto` (body) | Body scrolls internally instead of pushing the footer off-screen | | `border-b` / `border-t` | Visual separator so the pinned regions read as distinct | | `px-6 py-4` (body) / `px-6 pt-6 pb-3` (header) / `px-6 py-3` (footer) | Restore the padding that `p-0` removed, scoped to each region | ## Visual result ``` ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Header (Title) [pinned] │ ├──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Body content │ │ ↑ scrolls inside the dialog ↓ │ │ when the form is taller than 90vh │ ├──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Cancel Save [pinned] │ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` The dialog never extends below the viewport. The Save button is always one click away. ## Alternatives considered (rejected) - **`max-h-screen` instead of `max-h-[90vh]`** — touches the viewport edges; jarring. 90vh leaves backdrop visible. - **`overflow: auto` on `DialogContent` itself** — works, but the header scrolls out of view too. Worse UX. - **Sticky positioning** — `position: sticky` on header/footer works but is fragile across Radix's portal + transform-based animations. - **`fixed`-positioned footer outside `DialogContent`** — breaks Radix's focus trap. Don't. ## Example Domains | Domain | Long-form dialog | |--------|------------------| | ERP | Add / edit invoice with line items, payee, tax breakdown | | CRM | Edit lead — contact info, custom fields, tags, activity timeline | | Healthcare | Patient registration — demographics, insurance, history | | Project mgmt | Create epic — title, description, child issues, labels, assignees | | Inventory | Edit product — variants, pricing tiers, images, supplier links | | Admin panels | User edit — role grants, permission matrix, audit settings | ## Pitfalls - **Forgetting `p-0`** — default `DialogContent` has `p-6`; without removing it, you get padding around the entire scroll container, breaking the visual. - **`max-h-[90vh]` alone** without `flex flex-col` doesn't help — children still overflow. - **Nested `
` from react-hook-form** — `Form` doesn't impose layout, so the pattern works inside it. But if you wrap *everything* (header + body + footer) in a single ``, the form becomes the flex container — make sure `flex flex-col` is applied to the form itself, not its child. - **Mobile keyboard** — when a text input is focused on iOS, the keyboard pushes content up. `90vh` should still leave room for the footer; test if you support mobile. - **Multiple dialogs stacked** — each independent `` applies its own `max-h-[90vh]`; nesting is fine.

skills.name: rsync Deploy Protection in a Directory Shared with Human-Managed Files
skills.description: Your deploy script rsyncs a repo subtree into a directory that *also* contains files maintained outside the repo (a public landing page, ad-hoc uploads, a staging-only override). Without protection, every deploy clobbers those user-owned files. Two-line fix — `--exclude=<file>` for known overlaps, and `--backup-dir=$(date +%F-%H%M)` instead of `--suffix=.bak` so you keep a dated history rather than a single rotating buffer that the next deploy overwrites.
skills.body:
# rsync Deploy Protection in a Directory Shared with Human-Managed Files

## Problem

Your deploy script syncs a repo's `apps/foo/` subtree into `/var/www/foo/` on the host:

```bash
rsync -av "$SRC" /var/www/foo/
```

But `/var/www/foo/` also contains:
- `index.html` — the *public* landing page, edited by hand or via a CMS
- A few `.html` siblings the marketing team uploads through the file manager
- An `uploads/` directory with user-generated content
- A `.htaccess` or `robots.txt` that the operator tweaks

Every `git push` silently overwrites those files with whatever was last in the repo (usually a stale fixture, an empty stub, or — worse — nothing, because the file was never in the repo). The operator notices days later when the homepage looks wrong.

This is a classic deploy-shared-with-content trap. Three things compound it:

1. **The deploy uses `--suffix=.bak`** which is a *rotating buffer*: each deploy overwrites the previous `.bak` with the now-displaced version. After three deploys of the same content, the original is gone forever — `.bak` and live file are byte-identical.
2. **Nginx may serve the homepage from the deploy directory** via a `location = /` exact-match block (`root /var/www/foo; try_files /index.html =404;`). The deploy directory and the public-site root are the *same path* — nobody documented this.
3. **The operator's mental model says "the deploy only touches my app files"** — they didn't realize one of the deploy files happens to share a name with their public landing.

## Fix — two changes, both one-liners

### 1. `--exclude` the user-owned files

```bash
rsync -av \
  --exclude='index.html' \
  --exclude='robots.txt' \
  --exclude='uploads/' \
  --exclude='.htaccess' \
  "$SRC" /var/www/foo/
```

Pick the conservative default: anything that exists in the target *and* in the source where the canonical version lives in the target. Tag each with a comment so the next maintainer knows why:

```bash
rsync -av \
  --exclude='index.html' \   # public hopetech.me landing — owned outside repo
  --exclude='robots.txt' \   # operator-curated; do not regenerate
  "$SRC" /var/www/foo/
```

### 2. Replace `--suffix=.bak` with `--backup-dir=DATE/`

The single-suffix backup is worse than nothing because it gives a false sense of recoverability:

```bash
# bad — every deploy clobbers the previous backup
rsync -av --backup --suffix=.bak ...
```

```bash
# good — every deploy creates a dated tree of every overwritten file
rsync -av --backup --backup-dir="/var/backups/myapp/$(date +%F-%H%M%S)" ...
```

After three deploys you have:

```
/var/backups/myapp/2026-04-30-22-06-45/
/var/backups/myapp/2026-04-30-22-14-12/
/var/backups/myapp/2026-04-30-23-01-58/
```

Each contains *only* the files that were displaced at that deploy. To recover any version, `cp` from the right dated dir.

Add a retention sweeper to the same script:

```bash
# Keep last 30 deploys' backups; delete the rest.
find /var/backups/myapp -maxdepth 1 -type d -name '20*' \
  | sort -r | tail -n +31 | xargs -r rm -rf
```

## Detection — find these traps before they bite

When taking over a system, run this once per deploy directory:

```bash
# Files in the deploy dir that the deploy never writes (i.e. user-owned)
comm -23 \
  <(cd /var/www/foo && find . -type f | sort) \
  <(cd /repo/apps/foo && find . -type f | sort) | head
```

Anything in that list is at risk on every deploy. Either:
- Move it out of the deploy directory (preferred), OR
- `--exclude` it.

## Generalization

| Setup where this trap appears | What's at risk |
|---|---|
| nginx `root /var/www/app; location = / { try_files /index.html ...; }` | The public landing page lives in the same dir as the app's static assets |
| WordPress / Drupal alongside a repo-managed plugin | wp-config.php, uploads/, custom mu-plugins/ |
| Static-site generator output dir + hand-written 404.html | The 404 page gets clobbered every build |
| Container deploys mounting host dir with operator config | docker-compose overrides, .env, persistent data |
| Hostinger/cPanel managed VPS where multiple "apps" share `public_html/` | Every deploy script claims the whole dir |

## Anti-patterns

- **Don't** assume `--backup --suffix=.bak` gives you history. It gives you *one* generation, and the next deploy with no real change still rewrites it.
- **Don't** put `.gitkeep`-style markers in the deploy source to "claim" files in the target — that *adds* to the clobber surface.
- **Don't** rsync with `--delete` into a shared directory unless you've audited every file the operator might have added. `--delete` will silently remove their hand-uploaded files on the next sync.
- **Don't** "fix" it by moving the deploy target to a new dir without telling the operator — their nginx config, file manager bookmarks, and habits all assume the old path.
- **Don't** ship `index.html` in the deploy bundle if you've decided `index.html` is operator-owned. Removing the file from the repo is even safer than `--exclude` because it leaves no possibility of the rule being forgotten on a future deploy script rewrite.

## Recovery if you've already clobbered

If `--suffix=.bak` already gave you back-to-back identical deploys (live and `.bak` have the same MD5), the original is *gone from the deploy dir*. Look elsewhere on the host:

```bash
# Sibling directories under /var/www often hold predecessors
find /var/www -name "$(basename $LOST_FILE)" -size +5k 2>/dev/null

# Older backup roots still keep originals untouched
ls /var/www/<old-app-name>/   # e.g. /var/www/hopetech/ next to /var/www/bni/

# Nginx config may reveal a parallel-routed copy
grep -r "$(basename $LOST_FILE)" /etc/nginx/
```

The "look at the sibling directory under `/var/www`" tip recovers more lost landing pages than any other technique on managed VPS — operators often duplicate-then-edit when they migrate apps, leaving the predecessor next door.

skills.name: SCADA Real-Time ReactFlow — Complete Debugging Case Study
skills.description: 12-issue chain that prevented live PLC tag values from updating ReactFlow HMI elements. Documents every failure point and the final working architecture.
skills.body:
# SCADA Real-Time ReactFlow — Complete Debugging Case Study

## The Goal
Display live PLC tag values on a ReactFlow-based HMI screen viewer. When an operator toggles %M0 on a Schneider M221 PLC, a Gate Valve symbol should change from open (green) to closed (red) within 1 second.

## The Data Path (12 links, all must work)
```
1. Schneider M221 simulator (%M0 coil)
2. → WireGuard VPN tunnel (user PC → VPS)
3. → Modbus TCP read (polling engine on VPS)
4. → Tag Engine (in-memory, emits tagChange/tagUpdate)
5. → Socket.IO server (io.emit to all clients)
6. → nginx reverse proxy (WebSocket upgrade)
7. → Browser Socket.IO client (connects to WS_URL)
8. → Zustand realtime store (updateTagValue → tagVersion++)
9. → ScreenViewerPage (initialNodes useMemo depends on tagVersion)
10. → ReactFlow setNodes (new data object reference)
11. → PidSymbolNode memo'd component (receives new props)
12. → GateValve SVG (renders open/closed based on state prop)
```

## Every Issue Found (in order of discovery)

### Issue 1: ALLOWED_DEVICE_SUBNETS blocked localhost
- **Symptom**: "Host 127.0.0.1 is not in allowed subnets"
- **Fix**: Added `127.0.0.0/8` to `ALLOWED_DEVICE_SUBNETS` in `environment.ts`

### Issue 2: WS_URL defaulting to localhost in production
- **Symptom**: Socket.IO "connected" but 0 clients on server
- **Root cause**: `constants.ts` had `WS_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_WS_URL || 'http://localhost:3001'`. No env var set on Vercel.
- **Fix**: Auto-detect production: `isProduction ? 'https://api.nexaproc.in' : 'http://localhost:3001'`

### Issue 3: PM2 cluster mode split in-memory state
- **Symptom**: Polling started on worker A, Socket.IO clients on worker B, status check returns empty
- **Fix**: Run PM2 with single instance (`-i 1`), not cluster mode

### Issue 4: Socket.IO room subscription chain broken
- **Symptom**: Client connected but never received tag:update events
- **Root cause**: Server used `io.to('tag:UUID').emit()` but client never emitted `subscribe:tags` to join rooms
- **Fix**: Broadcast to ALL clients with `io.emit('tag:update', tagValue)` instead of room-only

### Issue 5: tagChange only fires on VALUE CHANGE
- **Symptom**: Client connected after initial value read, never received updates because value stayed constant
- **Root cause**: `tagEngine.on('tagChange')` only fires when value differs from previous. If coil stays true for 40 minutes, no events after first poll.
- **Fix**: Also broadcast on `tagEngine.on('tagUpdate')` which fires on EVERY poll cycle

### Issue 6: ScreenViewerPage's elementToNode missing tagBindings
- **Symptom**: Debug log showed `No bindings on node — keys: symbolComponent,symbolName,...` (no tagBindings key)
- **Root cause**: ScreenViewerPage had its OWN `elementToNode` function that NEVER included `tagBindings`, `animationRules`, `visibilityRule`, or `clickAction` in the node data
- **Fix**: Added all four fields to the P&ID symbol branch in `elementToNode`

### Issue 7: Valve state mapping — running/stopped vs open/closed
- **Symptom**: Valve disappeared when tag value changed
- **Root cause**: Boolean `true` mapped to `'running'` but GateValve only accepts `'open'|'closed'|'transit'|'fault'|'manual'|'offline'`. Unknown state = no render.
- **Fix**: Check `categoryKey === 'valves'` → map to `open/closed` instead of `running/stopped`

### Issue 8: Animation rules used tag NAME instead of UUID
- **Symptom**: Animation rules never matched — `tagValues.get('tag1')` returned undefined
- **Root cause**: Editor saved `tagId: 'tag1'` (name) but store keys are UUIDs
- **Fix**: Updated database directly via Prisma to replace tag names with UUIDs

### Issue 9: Demo simulation overwriting real-time values
- **Symptom**: Values correct on reload but never updated live
- **Root cause**: `hasRealData` was false (tag values hadn't arrived yet), so demo simulation interval ran every tick, overwriting any real-time state changes with random values
- **Fix**: `if (hasBindings) return;` — disable demo when real tag bindings exist

### Issue 10: Socket.IO ping timeout too aggressive
- **Symptom**: Client connected then disconnected within 2-4 seconds
- **Root cause**: `pingTimeout: 5000` (5 seconds) was too short for browser tab throttling + VPN latency
- **Fix**: Increased to `pingTimeout: 20000` (20 seconds). No security impact — ping is transport health check, not auth.

### Issue 11: useSocket hook disconnected on page navigation
- **Symptom**: Server logs showed `reason: client namespace disconnect` within 3 seconds of every connection
- **Root cause**: `useSocket` hook's cleanup function called `socketService.disconnect()` on component unmount. Every page navigation unmounted and remounted the layout.
- **Fix**: Removed cleanup disconnect. Socket stays alive across navigations. Only disconnects on explicit logout.

### Issue 12: React/ReactFlow re-rendering not triggered by setNodes
- **Symptom**: setInterval + setNodes didn't update the valve visually
- **Root cause**: Multiple competing approaches (interval in parent, useState in child, useMemo with Map dependency) all failed because ReactFlow's memo'd components need specific data flow.
- **Fix**: Resolve tag values INSIDE the `initialNodes` useMemo with `tagVersion` as dependency. When `tagVersion` increments (every tag:update), the entire node array recalculates with live values baked in, then `setNodes(canvasOnlyNodes)` runs — the same code path that works on reload.

## Final Working Architecture

```
Socket.IO event: tag:update
  → useRealtimeStore.updateTagValue() → tagVersion++
  → ScreenViewerPage: tagVersion selector triggers re-render
  → initialNodes useMemo([screen, tagVersion]) recalculates
    → elementToNode() creates node data
    → Tag values resolved from useRealtimeStore.getState().tagValues
    → Animation rules evaluated, state mapped (valves: open/closed)
  → canvasOnlyNodes derived from initialNodes
  → setNodes(canvasOnlyNodes) updates ReactFlow
  → PidSymbolNode receives new data.state prop
  → GateValve renders with new state color
```

## Key Principles Learned

1. **Trace the ENTIRE data path before fixing anything** — we fixed 12 issues one at a time over many deploys. Should have traced all 12 links upfront.

2. **ReactFlow memo'd components only re-render when node.data reference changes** — internal useState/useEffect/setInterval inside memo'd components gets swallowed.

3. **Never have competing intervals** — demo simulation and real-time interval both calling setNodes = chaos.

4. **Socket.IO rooms are complex** — for <100 tags, just `io.emit()` to all clients. Room subscription has too many failure points.

5. **useSocket cleanup should NOT disconnect** — socket connections are expensive to re-establish. Keep alive across page navigations.

6. **tagChange vs tagUpdate** — tagChange fires only on value CHANGE, tagUpdate fires on every poll. For real-time displays, broadcast on tagUpdate.

7. **Same code path for live and reload** — if reload works but live doesn't, make live use the SAME code path as reload (recalculate initialNodes, not patch nodes after creation).

skills.name: Screenshot-to-Root-Cause Error Diagnosis
skills.description: Decode minified React/production errors from browser screenshots — decode error URLs, trace stack traces, identify the actual component and data flow causing the crash
skills.body:
# Screenshot-to-Root-Cause Error Diagnosis

## Problem

Users share browser screenshots of production errors. The errors are minified and the stack traces reference bundled filenames like `index-Cv2HogrL.js:39:6327`. You need to trace this back to the actual source code and root cause.

## Diagnosis Workflow

### Step 1: Decode the Error

React minified errors include a URL with the error code and args:

```
https://reactjs.org/docs/error-decoder.html?invariant=31&args[]=object+with+keys+%7Bcode%2C+message%7D
```

Decode the URL params:
- `invariant=31` → React error #31
- `args[]` → URL-decode to get the actual message: "object with keys {code, message}"

Common React errors:
| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| #31 | Objects are not valid as a React child |
| #130 | Element type is invalid (wrong import) |
| #152 | Nothing was returned from render |
| #185 | Maximum update depth exceeded |
| #321 | Cannot update unmounted component |

### Step 2: Identify the Error Boundary

- **"Unexpected Application Error!"** → React Router's default error boundary (no custom `errorElement`)
- **"Something went wrong"** → Custom error boundary
- **White screen** → No error boundary at all

### Step 3: Trace the Component

1. Check which URL/route was loaded (from the browser address bar in the screenshot)
2. Find the route definition in `createBrowserRouter` or route config
3. Identify which component renders at that route
4. Read the component and check all JSX expressions `{variable}` for potential object rendering

### Step 4: Trace the Data Flow

For error #31 ("object rendered as child"), check:
1. All `useState` variables rendered in JSX — can any be set to an object?
2. All API error handlers — do they extract `.error` or `.message` as strings?
3. External data sources (localStorage, URL params, WebSocket) — can they return objects?
4. Proxy/CDN error responses — do they match the expected format?

### Step 5: Match the Object Shape

The error tells you the object's keys (e.g., `{code, message}`). Search for what produces that exact shape:
- `{code, message}` → proxy errors (Vercel, nginx), Zod issues, DOMException
- `{error, code}` → custom API error responses
- `{statusCode, message}` → HTTP framework errors (Express, Fastify)
- `{type, message}` → WebSocket errors, custom events

## Key Insight

The error is often NOT in the component's own code but in how external errors flow into rendered state. Check the full chain: API call → error response → catch block → setState → JSX render.

## When to Apply

- User shares a browser screenshot with a production error
- Error messages reference minified bundle filenames
- React "Minified error" messages in production

skills.name: Self-Updating Cron Script via Remote Fetch and Atomic Re-Exec
skills.description: A long-running cron script installed at `/usr/local/bin/foo.sh` is a frozen snapshot of the day it was installed — every logic change requires the user to re-run the install command, which they forget. Fix: at the start of every run, fetch the latest version from a known URL, atomic-replace `$0`, and `exec` the new version with a guard env-var to prevent re-update loops. Means logic improvements propagate within one cron tick of a `git push`, no user action required.
skills.body:
# Self-Updating Cron Script via Remote Fetch and Atomic Re-Exec

## Problem

You install a script as a per-minute cron:

```
* * * * * /usr/local/bin/myapp-deploy.sh
```

A week later you fix a bug in the script in your repo, push, and... nothing happens on the host. The cron is still running the **frozen snapshot** from the day you ran the install command. The user has to re-run the install command to pick up changes — and they forget.

This shows up everywhere:
- Deploy scripts that need to learn new logic
- Backup scripts where you fixed a bug
- Cron-driven scrapers / ETLs that need a new field
- Health-check scripts that need a new endpoint

## Pattern — fetch, atomic-replace, re-exec, with a re-entry guard

Add this block near the top of the script (after argument parsing, before the real work):

```bash
# ── self-update from canonical URL ────────────────────────────────────────
# Every run, pull the latest version of this file. If it differs, atomically
# replace ourselves and exec the new version. Skipped during the re-exec
# (NO_SELF_UPDATE=1) so we don't loop forever if the new file also differs.
if [ "${NO_SELF_UPDATE:-0}" != "1" ] && [ -w "$0" ]; then
  LATEST="$(curl -sL --max-time 10 "$UPDATE_URL" 2>/dev/null || true)"
  if [ -n "$LATEST" ]; then
    CUR="$(cat "$0" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    if [ "$LATEST" != "$CUR" ]; then
      printf '%s' "$LATEST" > "$0.new"
      chmod +x "$0.new"
      mv "$0.new" "$0"
      exec env NO_SELF_UPDATE=1 "$0" "$@"
    fi
  fi
fi
```

That's the entire pattern. Set `UPDATE_URL` near the top of your script:

```bash
UPDATE_URL="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<org>/<repo>/main/scripts/myapp-deploy.sh"
```

## Why each piece matters

| Piece | Reason |
|---|---|
| `NO_SELF_UPDATE=1` guard on re-exec | Without it, if the new file also "differs" because of timestamps or reformatting, you loop infinitely. The guard ensures self-update happens at most once per cron tick. |
| `[ -w "$0" ]` writability check | If `$0` is a symlink to a read-only path or a bin owned by another user, skip cleanly instead of erroring. |
| `--max-time 10` on curl | Cron ticks must finish quickly. Without a timeout, a hung curl blocks the whole cron run and stacks up. |
| `\|\| true` swallows curl error | A network blip should not crash the whole script — you want to fall through to the locally-cached copy. |
| `cat "$0" \|\| true` | Same: if the local file is somehow unreadable, fall through with `CUR=""` so the diff compares correctly. |
| `printf '%s' "$LATEST" > "$0.new"` then `mv` | Atomic replace. Never write directly to `$0` — a partial write during the upcoming `exec` would corrupt the file mid-execution. `mv` on the same filesystem is atomic. |
| `exec env NO_SELF_UPDATE=1 "$0" "$@"` | Replaces the shell process with the new script, preserving the original argv. The bash interpreter has already loaded the OLD script's text into memory, so we MUST re-exec to run the new code. |

## Variant: hash check before fetch (saves bandwidth on slow links)

```bash
LATEST_HASH="$(curl -sL --max-time 5 "$UPDATE_URL.sha256" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')"
LOCAL_HASH="$(sha256sum "$0" | awk '{print $1}')"
if [ -n "$LATEST_HASH" ] && [ "$LATEST_HASH" != "$LOCAL_HASH" ]; then
  # only NOW fetch the full file
  ...
fi
```

Most of the time, the script is already up to date and you only spend a 64-byte HTTP round-trip per tick instead of a several-KB script fetch.

## Generalization

| Domain | Why this fits |
|---|---|
| Deploy / sync scripts on customer-owned VPS | You can't ssh in to update them; this lets `git push` propagate logic changes |
| Edge-device update agents (IoT, Raspberry Pi fleets) | Devices behind NAT can't accept push; pull-and-self-replace is the only way |
| Cron-driven log shippers / metric collectors | Schema changes need to land everywhere within minutes |
| BBS / kiosk / digital-signage controllers | Same model — pull from a control URL, replace, re-exec |

## Anti-patterns

- **Don't** skip the `NO_SELF_UPDATE` guard. Network jitter, BOM bytes, line-ending differences can all make `LATEST != CUR` even when the content is "the same," and you'll loop.
- **Don't** write to `$0` directly. Bash has the file open for reading; depending on filesystem semantics, in-place truncation can corrupt the running interpreter's view.
- **Don't** verify with `diff -q` and a tempfile — that's an extra fork. The `[ "$LATEST" != "$CUR" ]` string compare is what you want.
- **Don't** chase the latest commit SHA via `git ls-remote` AND fetch the file content too — pick one. SHA-only is enough for "should I deploy?"; file-content compare is enough for "should I self-update?". Mixing both adds complexity for no benefit.
- **Don't** re-exec without `env`. The fresh process needs to inherit your normal cron env *plus* the guard flag — `env NO_SELF_UPDATE=1 "$0" "$@"` does exactly that, where bare `exec NO_SELF_UPDATE=1 "$0"` would either fail to set the env or trip up shellcheck.

## Companion skills

- `cron-poll-continuous-deploy` — the deploy-loop this self-update pattern was extracted from. The two compose: SHA-poll decides "is there a new commit to deploy?" and self-update decides "is there a new version of *me* to run?".

skills.name: shared-vps-coexistence
skills.description: Operational rules and procedures for safely adding a new product to a busy multi-tenant Linux VPS (Hostinger, DigitalOcean droplet, EC2, bare-metal) that already runs unrelated production-ish workloads. Covers port allocation, file namespacing, nginx site additions, docker compose isolation, blast-radius mitigations, and the survey-before-touch protocol.
skills.body:
# Shared-VPS Coexistence

## When to use

You are about to deploy a **new product** onto a Linux VPS that **already runs other unrelated products**. Examples that smell like this:

- Hostinger / OVH / Hetzner / Contabo VPS shared across many side-projects
- A "ops box" that the user uses as a personal cluster
- A staging host that grew organically and now fronts multiple internal tools
- Any host where `systemctl list-units --type=service` shows services from more than one product

If the host is dedicated to a single product, this skill does not apply — use a normal deployment skill instead.

## The core risk

Shared nginx, shared kernel, shared disk, shared docker daemon. One misconfigured config file, one `docker compose down --volumes`, one `rm -rf` in the wrong place takes down every product on the box, not just yours. The shared resources that matter most are, in order:

1. **nginx** — one bad site file or a missing `nginx -t` and the proxy refuses to reload (or worse, crashes), 502-ing every product
2. **docker daemon** — a project-name collision causes `docker compose down` from one repo to stop another product's containers
3. **disk** — one product's runaway log or backup fills `/` and crashes others
4. **ports** — silent collision on a publicly-bound port causes one of you to fail-to-bind on next restart

## Step 0 — Survey before touching anything

**Never** start writing files until you understand what's on the box. SSH in and run a strictly read-only survey:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/<key> -o BatchMode=yes <user>@<host> '
echo "=== CPU / RAM / DISK ==="
nproc; free -h; df -h / /var

echo "=== LISTENING PORTS ==="
ss -tlnp 2>/dev/null

echo "=== RUNNING SERVICES (non-system) ==="
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager --no-legend \
  | grep -v -E "^(systemd-|user@|polkit|ssh\.|cron\.|dbus\.|networkd|resolved|udev|rsyslog|chrony|getty)"

echo "=== DOCKER ==="
docker ps -a --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
docker compose ls

echo "=== REVERSE PROXY ==="
for p in nginx caddy traefik apache2 httpd haproxy; do which $p && echo "-- $p installed"; done
ls /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ 2>/dev/null
ls /etc/caddy/ 2>/dev/null

echo "=== LETSENCRYPT CERTS ==="
ls /etc/letsencrypt/live/ 2>/dev/null

echo "=== USER DIRS / /opt ==="
ls -la /home /opt /root

echo "=== FIREWALL ==="
ufw status 2>/dev/null || iptables -S INPUT 2>/dev/null
'
```

Capture this output **in writing** — paste it into your project's RUNBOOK or design doc — so future you knows the starting state. The most important deliverable from Step 0 is a list of:

- Every listening port (TCP and UDP)
- Every `/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*` file name
- Every Docker compose project name (`docker compose ls`)
- Disk % used
- Tenants/products you have to not break

## Step 1 — Pick names that namespace cleanly

| Resource | Convention |
|---|---|
| Docker compose project | `<product>` (verified absent in `docker compose ls`) |
| Service files dir | `/opt/<product>/` (verified `/opt/<product>` absent in `ls /opt`) |
| Logs dir | `/var/log/<product>/` |
| nginx site file | `/etc/nginx/sites-available/<product>` symlinked from `sites-enabled/<product>` |
| Cron scripts | `/etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly}/<product>-<purpose>` |
| Systemd units | `<product>-<service>.service` |
| System user | `<product>` (a dedicated, non-root, system user) |
| Sysctl drops | `/etc/sysctl.d/99-<product>-<purpose>.conf` |

The point is that any future operator can `grep -r <product>` and find everything you touched, while everything you did **not** touch is plainly someone else's.

## Step 2 — Allocate a port range on loopback only

Pick a contiguous unused range (verify via `ss -tlnp` from Step 0). Bind every internal service to `127.0.0.1` only — **nothing** of yours listens on `0.0.0.0` or `::`. Public traffic enters only through the shared nginx on 80/443.

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml fragment — bind to loopback explicitly
services:
  api:
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:54330:8080"   # NOT "54330:8080"
```

Common pitfall: forgetting the `127.0.0.1:` prefix in `ports:` makes the service public on all interfaces. UFW may not save you because Docker bypasses it via iptables rules it installs itself.

## Step 3 — Add the nginx site with three mitigations

The shared nginx is the highest-risk shared resource. Apply all three:

1. **Touch only your own site file.** Never edit `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` (shared), never edit any other tenant's site file. New file lives at `/etc/nginx/sites-available/<product>` only.
2. **`nginx -t` before every reload.** The test parses the entire config (including other tenants' files). If your file has a typo, the test fails non-zero and you fix it before reloading. Reloading without a successful test is the most common way to break a shared proxy.
3. **Commit the site file to your product's git repo** at `deploy/nginx/<product>.conf`. Two benefits: diff review before deploy, fast rollback after.

```bash
# Standard sequence on the VPS
sudo cp deploy/nginx/<product>.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/<product>
sudo ln -sfn /etc/nginx/sites-available/<product> /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/<product>
sudo nginx -t        # MUST exit 0 before next line
sudo nginx -s reload # graceful — existing connections drain on old workers
```

If `nginx -t` fails after your edit, the rest of the system is untouched. Fix the typo, retest, then reload.

## Step 4 — Docker compose: project name and volume safety

Set the project name explicitly to your product name so other tenants' `docker compose down` cannot match your containers:

```bash
# In /opt/<product>/.env or compose-up wrapper
export COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=<product>
```

**Never** `docker compose down --volumes` on a shared host without a fresh backup. The flag silently removes named volumes — months of DB state gone. Document in RUNBOOK that `--volumes` is forbidden unless paired with an explicit backup step.

## Step 5 — Disk pressure guardrail

Shared disk is the slowest-failing shared resource — it gets fuller over time and crashes everyone at once. Install an hourly disk-check before bringing real workloads up:

```bash
# /etc/cron.hourly/<product>-disk-check
#!/bin/bash
set -u
THRESHOLD=85
LOG=/var/log/<product>/disk-alert.log
TS=$(date -Iseconds)
USED=$(df -h / | awk 'NR==2 {print $5}' | tr -d %)

if [ -n "$USED" ] && [ "$USED" -ge "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
  MSG="[<product>] disk-pressure: / at ${USED}% (threshold ${THRESHOLD}%)"
  echo "$TS $MSG" >> "$LOG"
  logger -t <product>-disk-check -p user.warning "$MSG"
fi
exit 0
```

Make executable (`chmod 0755`), `cron.hourly` picks it up automatically. To wire it to Slack / Discord / email later, append a `curl` call below the `logger` line — keep the threshold logic intact.

## Step 6 — Memory: add swap before bringing heavyweight workloads up

On a shared host with no swap, one OOM cascades — the kernel will kill processes from any tenant. Adding swap is a one-time, idempotent operation:

```bash
if ! swapon --show=NAME --noheadings | grep -qx /swapfile; then
  fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
  chmod 600 /swapfile
  mkswap /swapfile
  swapon /swapfile
fi
grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*/swapfile' /etc/fstab \
  || printf '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0\n' >> /etc/fstab
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/99-<product>-swap.conf <<EOF
vm.swappiness=10
EOF
sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-<product>-swap.conf
```

`swappiness=10` keeps the kernel preferring RAM (avoids needless paging) but allows swap as an OOM safety net.

## Step 7 — Author a RUNBOOK before the product runs

Write `/opt/<product>/RUNBOOK.md` *before* the first deploy, not after the first incident. Include:

- The coexistence rules from this skill
- Routine maintenance crons (docker prune, log rotate, disk check)
- Disk-pressure response procedure
- Service start/stop commands
- Restore-from-backup procedure
- Decommission procedure

Also commit a copy at `deploy/RUNBOOK.md` in the product's repo and add a CI check that the two are in sync (or document that they may drift and how to reconcile).

## Smell tests — when this skill is not enough

- The shared host already has > 50% sustained CPU before your product. → Pick a different host.
- The shared host is < 90% reachable in your monitoring. → Pick a different host.
- Other tenants on the host are production-customer-facing and your product is dev/staging. → Pick a different host or get explicit alignment with those tenants' owners.

## Anti-patterns

- ❌ Editing `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` instead of a per-product `sites-available/` file
- ❌ Skipping `nginx -t` because "it's only one line"
- ❌ Binding to `0.0.0.0` "just to test"
- ❌ Reusing another tenant's Docker network or volume
- ❌ Writing logs to `/var/log/syslog` only (gets mixed with the world)
- ❌ Running `docker system prune -af --volumes` without coordination — kills *everyone's* volumes
- ❌ Skipping the survey "because the box is mine"

skills.name: silent-out-of-scope-no-enumeration
skills.body:
# Silent Out-of-Scope — Never Enumerate What's Excluded

## Skill Metadata
```yaml
name: Silent Out-of-Scope — Never Enumerate What's Excluded
description: In a client proposal, never enumerate specific features as "out of scope" or "not included". Listing exclusions plants ideas the client didn't ask for, invites change-request friction, and signals that you considered (but did not deliver) more than was contracted. Replace itemised exclusion lists with a single generic change-control clause.
version: 1.0.0
tags: [proposals, scope, copywriting, change-control, client-management]
```

## Problem

It is tempting in a proposal's Terms section to write:

> "Change control. Material additions outside the six deliverables (e.g. WhatsApp two-way, GeM portal scraping, ERP invoicing, live GST/CIN APIs) require a written change request and are not in Phase-1 scope."

Or in a footnote on the commercials page:

> "Commercial terms — rates, totals, taxes, payment schedule — are intentionally omitted from this proposal at the client's request."

Both feel "defensive and clear" to the author. To the client they read very differently:

1. **The enumerated list plants ideas.** A client who had not even thought of WhatsApp integration now asks "wait, could you add WhatsApp?" — and every line in the list becomes a future negotiation prompt.
2. **Mentioning what's NOT there draws attention to it.** Clients tend to mentally retain "missing" items more than "included" ones (negativity bias). A silent omission is forgotten; an explicit omission is remembered.
3. **The negotiation framing is wrong.** A change-request clause should describe the *process*, not the *list of features the process applies to*.
4. **Explicit "we deliberately omitted X at your request" looks like passive-aggressive bookkeeping.** It signals the relationship has friction. Better to simply not mention X.

## Solution

Apply the **silent-omission principle**: if something is not in scope, it does not appear in the proposal at all. The proposal describes only what IS being delivered. A single generic clause covers the change-control process.

### Rewrite pattern — Terms section

**BEFORE (enumerated):**
> Change control. Material additions outside the six deliverables (e.g. WhatsApp two-way, GeM portal scraping, ERP invoicing, live GST/CIN APIs) require a written change request and are not in Phase-1 scope.

**AFTER (silent):**
> Change control. Material additions outside the six deliverables follow a written change-request process.

That's it. No examples, no list, no "not in Phase-1" qualifier.

### Rewrite pattern — Commercials footnote

**BEFORE (explanatory):**
> Commercial terms — rates, totals, taxes, payment schedule — are intentionally omitted from this proposal at the client's request and will be issued as a separate commercial annex on demand.

**AFTER (silent):**
*Delete the entire footnote.* The page simply has no commercials. The client knows why — they asked for it. The proposal does not need to explain its own absences.

### Rewrite pattern — Phase boundary

**BEFORE (defensive):**
> Stage 9 (PO Receipt & Handover) is reserved for a separate Phase-2 engagement.

**AFTER (positive scope):**
> Scope is anchored to the 9-stage workflow set out in [reference document], with Phase 1 covering Stages 1–8.

The Phase-2 framing is implicit, not named.

## What stays in the proposal

- Everything that IS delivered (deliverables list, timeline, milestones, terms about what's included).
- The change-control PROCESS (generic clause — no list).
- Engagement boundaries phrased as positive scope ("Phase 1 covers Stages 1–8") not negative scope ("Phase 2 is not included").

## What never appears in the proposal

- Enumerated lists of out-of-scope features.
- "Intentionally omitted" footnotes.
- "Reserved for future phase" language with specific reservations.
- "Excluded: …" sections.
- "Not included in this engagement: …" lines.
- Any sentence whose function is to explain the absence of something.

## Example Domains

| Domain | Tempting exclusion list | Silent replacement |
|--------|------------------------|---------------------|
| Software consultancy | "Out of scope: SSO, WhatsApp, ERP, mobile app" | "Material additions follow a change-request process." |
| Architecture firm | "Excluded: landscape design, exterior signage, fit-out beyond Floor 2" | Scope statement covers Floor 2 — silence on the rest |
| Marketing agency | "Not included: print collateral, OOH, paid social" | Scope lists digital + content; no exclusion list |
| Legal services | "Out of retainer: litigation, M&A, IP filings" | Retainer lists what's covered; no list of what's not |
| Healthcare contract | "Excluded procedures: cardiac, oncology, transplant" | Service catalogue lists covered procedures only |
| Construction tender | "Items by Others: HVAC, plumbing, electrical to second fix" | Boundary drawing — silent on what's by Others |

## Internal scope docs are different

This discipline applies to **client-facing proposals and contracts**. The internal scope document, the engineering plan, the project management RACI — those *must* enumerate exclusions because the delivery team needs to know what they're not building. Keep two artefacts:

- `*_proposal.html` / `*_contract.docx` → silent on exclusions.
- `*_scope_internal.md` / `*_runbook.md` → explicit exclusion list.

## When you must mention something not delivered

Rare cases force an explicit reference (regulatory disclosure, prior contract amendment, etc.). Even then, prefer positive framing:

- **Avoid:** "This proposal does not include audit & assurance."
- **Prefer:** "Audit & assurance is delivered under our separate engagement letter dated [X]."

## Anti-patterns

- **The "for clarity" exclusion list.** "For clarity, the following are out of scope: …" — these never add clarity. They add ammunition for change-request bargaining.
- **The footnote that explains why a section is empty.** If the section is empty, leave it empty. The reader's eye skips empty sections; a footnote draws their gaze straight to the void.
- **Naming the next phase's deliverables.** Don't write "Phase 2 will cover X, Y, Z" — you commit yourself to something not yet quoted. Say "Phase 2 will be scoped separately."
- **Listing technologies you considered and rejected.** "We evaluated Tech A but chose Tech B" reads as second-guessing. State the chosen stack; the rejected one is internal.
- **The pre-emptive "we cannot do X" clause.** Either you cannot (in which case why is the client talking to you) or it is out of scope (in which case silence). Pre-emptive limitation language signals weakness.

## Key Rule

**Describe what you will deliver. Stay silent on everything else. A single generic change-control clause covers all future additions. Never enumerate — enumeration is invitation.**

skills.name: slack-bot-permanent-on-macos-launchd
skills.description: Run a Slack bot 24/7 on your Mac without deploying to cloud. Uses @slack/bolt Socket Mode (no inbound port needed) wrapped in a launchd plist that auto-restarts on crash and survives reboot.
skills.body:
# Slack Bot 24/7 on macOS via launchd

## Problem
You built a Slack bot for internal/personal use and want it always-on. Cloud deploy (Vercel/Fly/Railway) adds cost, requires public webhook URLs, and complicates secret management. For a bot that only your team uses, running it on your Mac via launchd is faster, free, and lets you iterate locally.

## When to use
- Personal/team bots (under ~50 users)
- Bot needs access to local filesystem (vault, notes folder, downloads)
- You don't want to manage public webhook URLs
- Your Mac is "always on" enough (laptops sleep, but bot wakes immediately on lid open)

## When NOT to use
- Customer-facing bots — use Vercel/Fly
- Bots that must respond within seconds even when your Mac is asleep
- Compliance environments where production code can't run on a workstation

## Architecture
Slack's **Socket Mode** lets a bot connect outbound to Slack via WebSocket — no inbound HTTP needed. Pair this with macOS **launchd** to keep the Node process alive forever.

## Slack app setup (one-time)
1. api.slack.com/apps → Create New App (from scratch)
2. **Socket Mode** → Enable → generate App-Level Token with scope `connections:write` → save as `SLACK_APP_TOKEN` (starts with `xapp-`)
3. **OAuth & Permissions** → Bot Token Scopes: add at least `app_mentions:read`, `chat:write`, `im:history`, `im:write`, `channels:history`, `files:read`
4. **Event Subscriptions** → Enable → Subscribe to bot events: `app_mention`, `message.im`, `message.channels`
5. **App Home** → Messages Tab ON + check "Allow users to send Slash commands and messages from the messages tab"
6. **Install to Workspace** → copy Bot Token (`xoxb-...`)

## Code
```js
// bot.mjs
import { App } from '@slack/bolt';

const app = new App({
  token:        process.env.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN,
  appToken:     process.env.SLACK_APP_TOKEN,
  signingSecret: process.env.SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET,
  socketMode: true,
});

app.event('app_mention', async ({ event, say }) => {
  await say({ text: `Hi <@${event.user}>!`, thread_ts: event.ts });
});

app.event('message', async ({ event, client }) => {
  if (event.channel_type !== 'im' || event.bot_id) return;
  await client.chat.postMessage({ channel: event.channel, text: 'Got it' });
});

await app.start();
console.log('⚡ Bot running in Socket Mode');
```

## launchd plist
Save as `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.YOU.bot.plist` (replace `YOU` and paths):

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>          <string>com.YOU.bot</string>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key> <string>/Users/YOU/path/to/project</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/opt/homebrew/bin/node</string>
    <string>--env-file=.env.local</string>
    <string>bot.mjs</string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key>      <true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key>      <true/>
  <key>ThrottleInterval</key><integer>10</integer>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/tmp/bot.out.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/tmp/bot.err.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
```

## Load it
```bash
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.YOU.bot.plist
# Verify
launchctl list | grep bot
# Logs
tail -f /tmp/bot.out.log
```

## Reload after code changes
```bash
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.YOU.bot
```

## Common gotchas
- **node not found** — use absolute path (`/opt/homebrew/bin/node` on Apple Silicon, `/usr/local/bin/node` on Intel). `launchd` runs without your shell's PATH.
- **`.env` not loaded** — use `node --env-file=.env.local` flag (Node 20+) instead of `dotenv` so launchd's stripped env doesn't matter.
- **Two bots running** — `launchctl load` while a manual `node` is still running creates duplicates. Always `pkill -f bot.mjs` before reload.
- **Throttle wait** — if `KeepAlive: true` and your bot crashes immediately, launchd backs off. Use `ThrottleInterval: 10` to retry after 10s instead of growing exponential delay.
- **Lid-closed sleep** — bot pauses while Mac sleeps. Acceptable for most use cases. If not: keep Mac plugged in + System Settings → Battery → Power Adapter → "Prevent automatic sleeping when display is off".

## Verify it survives reboot
```bash
sudo shutdown -r now
# After login:
launchctl list | grep bot   # should show PID > 0
```

skills.name: Soft-Delete via hidden Flag for Reversible Dedupe
skills.description: Instead of `delete from`, mark duplicate or stale records with `hidden=true` and have every list view filter `hidden=false` by default with an opt-in "Show hidden" toggle. Lets you collapse 10+ duplicate name groups in a CRM/contact-list with a single re-runnable SQL file, keeps every record recoverable with a one-line UPDATE, and gives auditors a full-history view without needing tombstone tables.
skills.body:
# Soft-Delete via hidden Flag for Reversible Dedupe

## Problem

A long-running CRM / directory / catalog accumulates duplicates:

- Same person added twice with slightly different name spelling
- Bulk imports run twice
- Different teams enter the same lead with different IDs

You need to clean up but:

1. **`DELETE FROM` is irreversible** — no undo if you picked the wrong canonical record.
2. **Foreign keys break** — child rows (notes, activities, follow-ups) reference the deleted ID and either ON-DELETE-cascade away (data loss) or block the delete entirely.
3. **Users still want an audit view** — "show me everyone we've ever added, including duplicates I've cleaned up."

## Pattern — `hidden boolean` column + UI filter

### Schema

```sql
alter table app_contacts
  add column if not exists hidden boolean not null default false;

create index if not exists app_contacts_hidden_idx
  on app_contacts (hidden) where hidden = false;
```

(Partial index: most queries are `where hidden=false`, so indexing only the visible rows keeps it tiny.)

### Dedupe migration — explicit canonical pick per group

```sql
-- dedupe_contacts.sql — re-runnable; sets state explicitly per group.
-- Each block: keep one canonical record visible, hide the rest.

-- 1. Reshma Dave: keep c68 (most complete record, status=Met, has phone).
update app_contacts set hidden=false where id='c68';
update app_contacts set hidden=true  where id in ('c23','c33');

-- 2. Prakruti Verma: keep c66.
update app_contacts set hidden=false where id='c66';
update app_contacts set hidden=true  where id in ('c22','c67');

-- ... one block per duplicate group
```

Why explicit `set hidden=false` on the canonical too: the file becomes idempotent and self-documenting. Re-running it always lands the system in the same state, even if someone manually flipped a flag in between.

### List queries — default to hidden=false

```sql
select * from app_contacts where hidden = false order by ...;
```

### UI — opt-in toggle

```html
<label>
  <input type="checkbox" id="showHidden" />
  Show hidden duplicates
</label>
```

```js
function getFiltered() {
  const showHidden = !!document.getElementById('showHidden').checked;
  return rows.filter(r => showHidden || !r.hidden);
}
```

## Why this beats the alternatives

| Approach | Reversible? | FK-safe? | Audit view? | Schema cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DELETE FROM` | No | No (cascades or blocks) | No | Free |
| Move to `_archived` table | Yes (manual restore) | No (still breaks FKs) | Two-table query | Mirror table per entity |
| `deleted_at timestamp` | Yes | Yes | Yes (with WHERE) | One column |
| **`hidden boolean`** | **Yes (one UPDATE)** | **Yes** | **Yes (toggle filter)** | **One column** |

`deleted_at timestamp` and `hidden boolean` are equivalent in safety; pick `hidden` when the flag is the user-facing concept (CRM "hide from views") and `deleted_at` when the flag is the audit-trail concept ("when was this archived").

## Generalization

| Domain | Soft-delete fits when |
|---|---|
| CRM / contact directory | Duplicate leads from imports |
| Product catalog | Discontinued SKUs you may re-list |
| Knowledge base / doc CMS | Old versions kept for history |
| Multi-tenant config | Tenant offboarding (reversible suspend) |
| Feature-flag rollouts | Soft-removed flags before final cleanup |

## Anti-patterns

- **Don't** mix `hidden` and `deleted_at` on the same table — pick one. Two flags is two ways for state to drift.
- **Don't** add an `is_active` column with the opposite polarity — `hidden=false` is mentally easier to reason about than `is_active=true` when reading WHERE clauses.
- **Don't** build a magic global RLS policy that filters `hidden=true` — explicit `where hidden=false` in queries is greppable; an invisible RLS rule isn't.
- **Don't** forget the partial index — without it, every list query scans hidden rows you'll never use.

## Companion artifact: include verification SQL

End the dedupe file with a commented-out verification query so the next person running it can sanity-check:

```sql
-- After running, you should see one row per real person.
-- select id, first, last, status from app_contacts
-- where status in ('active','engaged') and hidden = false
-- order by last, first;
```

skills.name: static-file-swap-stable-url
skills.description: To replace a document/asset's content without breaking any existing links, share URLs, or database pointers, overwrite the file at the SAME path rather than uploading a new one. Use when a PDF, image, HTML, or other static asset is referenced from many places (tracker rows, emails, embedded iframes, database `filename` columns) and you need to update the content silently. The stable URL is the contract; the file bytes are the variable.
skills.body:
# Static File Swap Under a Stable URL

A document is referenced from many places — a tracker row's `filename` column, prior emails to the client, embedded `<iframe>` in another page, bookmarks on the recipient's machine. You need to update the document's content. **Don't upload a new file with a new name** — every existing reference would break. Instead, overwrite the file bytes at the existing path. The URL stays stable; the content silently refreshes.

## The pattern

```
/public/documents/Proposal_2026_v1.pdf          ← stable URL referenced everywhere
     ↑ overwrite the file at this path
     ↑ commit + push (or rsync to server)
     ↑ deploy
     → every link, embed, DB pointer now serves the new content
```

## Why this is right (and the alternatives are wrong)

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| **Overwrite at same path** (this skill) | Zero churn elsewhere. All references keep working. Auditable via git diff. | Caches may still serve the old bytes briefly (handle with cache-bust). |
| Upload as new file + update DB pointer | Clean history of versions. | Every external reference (emails sent, bookmarks, embeds) silently breaks unless you also redirect old → new. |
| Attach as a "new version" in a versions table | Audit trail. | The row's primary `View` link doesn't change unless you update the pointer, defeating the swap. |

Mix-and-match: do the swap for the primary `View/Download` URL **and** also append a version row for the audit trail. Best of both.

## Implementation steps

1. **Locate every storage location** for the file. There are usually two:
   - The deployment-served copy (`public/documents/<name>.pdf`, `s3://bucket/path/<name>.pdf`, `nginx /var/www/files/<name>.pdf`)
   - The operator-facing source copy in the repo root or a build folder

2. **Overwrite both** with the new bytes. Keep the filename byte-identical.

3. **Verify the bytes changed** before pushing:
   ```bash
   sha256sum old/Proposal_2026_v1.pdf  new/Proposal_2026_v1.pdf
   # The two hashes must differ. If they match, you didn't actually swap.
   ```

4. **Ship through your normal deploy path.** Don't bypass with manual upload — you want the deploy artifact and git history to reflect the new bytes.

5. **Bust caches** when probing:
   ```bash
   curl -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{size_download}\n" \
     "https://example.com/documents/Proposal_2026_v1.pdf?cb=$(date +%s)"
   # `size_download` should match the new file size, not the old.
   ```

   The `?cb=` query param bypasses CDN caching for the probe. The browser may still serve the old bytes from its disk cache — instruct the recipient to **hard-refresh** (Cmd+Shift+R / Ctrl+F5) if they had previously opened the old version.

## Edge cases

**Browser/CDN caches.** Aggressive `Cache-Control: public, max-age=...` headers will keep the old bytes around. Either:
- Lower the cache TTL on these paths in your CDN config, or
- Add a versioned query string when linking (`?v=2026-06-02`) — only useful if you control the link generation everywhere.

**Read-only runtime filesystems** (Vercel functions, Lambda, App Engine standard, etc.). You can't write to `public/` at request time. The swap must happen at build/deploy time — i.e., committed to git and shipped through the pipeline. This is actually a strength: the bytes are version-controlled.

**Concurrent readers.** If a recipient downloads the file mid-deploy, they may get partial content. Most static-file servers handle this atomically (`mv` / rename is atomic on POSIX) but check your hosting platform's behaviour for large files.

**Audit trail.** Git history gives you the "who/when/what" automatically. If you also need the prior bytes recoverable in-app (not just via git), additionally write a row to a `versions` table snapshotting the old `file_path` / `sha256` before the swap.

## Example Domains

| Surface | Stable URL | What gets swapped |
|---------|-----------|-------------------|
| Internal proposal tracker (`/documents/<file>.pdf`) | DB column points at filename | The PDF bytes |
| Marketing site PDF download (`/whitepapers/security-overview.pdf`) | Linked from emails, blog posts, partner sites | The PDF bytes |
| Onboarding video CDN URL | Embedded in product, in emails | The video file at the same key |
| Brand assets (`/logos/wordmark.svg`) | Embedded in dozens of partner sites and exported decks | The SVG file |
| Public RSS / JSON feeds | Subscribers polling a fixed URL | The feed content |

## When NOT to use

- The change is breaking (renamed fields in a JSON feed, video aspect ratio change) — then a new URL with a deprecation period is better.
- You need both versions live simultaneously (A/B test, legal old-copy archive) — keep them as separate files.
- Compliance requires immutable storage (audit, regulatory) — use content-addressable storage where the URL IS the hash; never swap.

skills.name: Subscription vs Pay-As-You-Go API Key Billing Mismatch (Insufficient-Balance Despite Valid Plan)
skills.description: When a SaaS / LLM provider returns "insufficient balance" or 4xx-billing errors despite an active, paid subscription, the most common cause is an API key minted in a different billing context (pay-as-you-go wallet, prior tenant, or before the subscription was attached). The dashboard shows the plan as Valid with full quota, but API calls draw from an empty sub-wallet. Diagnosis is to check usage = 0% on the subscription quota dashboard, then regenerate the key under the active plan. Applies to Z.AI, OpenAI tiers, Anthropic team plans, Stripe, Twilio, GitHub apps, etc.
skills.body:
# Subscription vs Pay-As-You-Go API Key Billing Mismatch

## Symptom

Provider returns one of:
- HTTP 429 / 403 with body `"Insufficient balance"`, `"Quota exceeded"`, `"No active plan"`, error code `1113` (Z.AI), `insufficient_quota` (OpenAI), or similar
- All requests fail with the same billing-flavored message regardless of model, payload, or endpoint variation

But:
- Account dashboard shows subscription is **Valid** / **Active**
- Subscription's quota meter shows **0% used** even after many failed attempts
- Pay-as-you-go wallet (if separate) may have credit but isn't being drawn from

## Root cause

Many SaaS providers maintain **separate billing contexts** for:
1. **Pay-as-you-go wallet** - prepaid cash/credit balance, charged per call
2. **Subscription quota** - flat-rate plan, charged monthly, with usage caps
3. **Trial credits** / promotional balance
4. **Per-team / per-org** billing pools

API keys are **bound to the billing context that existed when the key was created.**
A key minted under pay-as-you-go does NOT auto-rebind when the user later subscribes
to a plan. The key continues drawing from its original (often empty) wallet.

## Diagnosis (in order)

1. **Check the usage dashboard for the subscription, not the wallet.** If subscription
   quota shows 0% / 0% / 0% used despite many failed call attempts, the calls aren't
   reaching the subscription's billing path.

2. **Compare the API key creation date to the subscription start date.** If key
   predates subscription, it's almost certainly bound to the older context.

3. **Probe with multiple model names / endpoints** to confirm the error is uniform
   across all paths. If yes, it's billing-context, not request-format.

4. **Check the docs for "supported tools" / "subscription gating"** language.
   Some providers (Z.AI Coding Plan, Anthropic Team plans) only honor subscription
   quotas when called via specific tools or endpoints.

## Fix

**Regenerate the API key while the subscription is active.** The new key is minted
under the current billing context and binds to subscription quota.

1. Open the provider's API key management page
2. Delete or rotate the old key
3. Create a new key
4. Update wherever the key is stored (env vars, settings files, CI secrets, vault)
5. Test with a single small request - should return 200 immediately

## Why providers don't auto-rebind

- Auditability - rebinding silently changes who pays for what
- Multi-tenant safety - keys may be shared across teammates with different plans
- Backwards compatibility - old keys keep working in their original context until rotated

This is a feature, not a bug. But the error messages rarely explain it.

## Variants by provider

| Provider | Symptom | Where to regenerate |
|----------|---------|---------------------|
| Z.AI / Zhipu (GLM Coding Plan) | error 1113 "Insufficient Balance" despite Valid plan | https://z.ai/manage-apikey/apikey-list |
| OpenAI (Team / Plus tier) | "insufficient_quota" while team has credits | https://platform.openai.com/api-keys |
| Anthropic (Team plan) | API returns 401/403 even after team admin grants access | https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys |
| Stripe (test vs live) | "No such customer" - key from wrong mode | https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys |
| Twilio (subaccount) | "Authentication failed" - parent vs subaccount key | Twilio Console - API Keys |

## Example Domains

| Domain | Applies? |
|--------|----------|
| LLM provider with subscription + PAYG tiers (Z.AI, OpenAI, Anthropic) | Yes - primary case |
| Payment APIs with test/live mode segregation (Stripe) | Yes - test keys hit test data only |
| Multi-tenant SaaS with sub-account keys (Twilio, AWS sub-accounts) | Yes - parent account keys don't access subaccount resources |
| GitHub Apps vs personal access tokens | Yes - app permissions differ from PAT scopes |
| Cloud KMS keys across projects/regions | Yes - key bound to creation project |

## Anti-patterns

- Adding more credit / topping up the wrong wallet - doesn't help when key isn't bound to it.
- Assuming "subscription Valid" on the dashboard means "all keys honor it" - rarely true without rebinding.
- Contacting support before regenerating the key - support's first answer is usually "regenerate the key."
- Building elaborate retry logic for what's actually a one-line fix.

## When regeneration doesn't fix it

Then the cause is elsewhere:

1. Subscription billing actually failed silently (auto-renew failed, payment method expired)
2. Key tier doesn't match endpoint requirements (e.g., free-tier key calling paid-only model)
3. Geographic / regulatory block (region-restricted models)
4. Account was flagged for ToS violation

In that order of likelihood. Check the billing history page first.

skills.name: Supabase Polling Overload — Diagnosis and Fix
skills.description: When Supabase shows millions of DB requests from a React app, the cause is almost always cascading React Query refetchIntervals and unguarded staleTime. Diagnose by grepping for refetchInterval, fix by raising intervals and adding staleTime.
skills.body:
# Supabase Polling Overload — Diagnosis and Fix

## The Symptom

Supabase dashboard shows millions of **database requests** in 24-30 hours. The split is almost entirely database requests (99%+), not API or storage. Cost and rate limits are at risk.

Real example: **10,924,194 database requests in 30 hours** (~101 req/sec sustained) on a hospital management app.

## Root Causes (in order of severity)

### 1. React Query `refetchInterval` too aggressive
Every open browser tab or mounted component runs the interval independently. Multiple users × multiple pages × short intervals = exponential load.

```ts
// WRONG — runs every 5 seconds per tab
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['sync-status'],
  queryFn: () => supabase.from('tally_sync_status').select('*'),
  refetchInterval: 5000,  // ← culprit
})

// CORRECT — 60 seconds minimum for status polling
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['sync-status'],
  queryFn: () => supabase.from('tally_sync_status').select('*'),
  refetchInterval: 60000,
})
```

**Rule of thumb:** Status/queue polling → 60s minimum. Approvals dashboard → 120s minimum.

### 2. Multiple independent polling queries on one page
A single page with 4 queries at 15-30s each = 8-16 req/min per user on that page.

```ts
// BillApprovals pattern — 4 queries each running independently
refetchInterval: 15000,  // pending bills
refetchInterval: 30000,  // approved bills
refetchInterval: 15000,  // pending discounts
refetchInterval: 15000,  // pending packages
// Total: ~8 req/min per user × concurrent users
```

Fix: Raise all to 120000 (2 minutes). Approval queues don't need sub-minute freshness.

### 3. Missing `staleTime` on app-root count queries
Count queries mounted at app root (sidebar badges, navigation counts) re-run on every route change without `staleTime`.

```ts
// 18 count queries running on every route navigation
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['diagnoses-count'],
  queryFn: () => supabase.from('diagnoses').select('count'),
  refetchOnWindowFocus: false,
  // missing staleTime → refetches on every route mount
})

// CORRECT
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['diagnoses-count'],
  queryFn: () => supabase.from('diagnoses').select('count'),
  refetchOnWindowFocus: false,
  staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000,  // ← holds for 5 min
})
```

### 4. Realtime subscription calling full refetch on every change
```ts
// WRONG — refetches all data on every single INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
supabase.channel('corporate-changes')
  .on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', table: 'corporate' }, () => {
    fetchCorporateData()  // ← called for every row in a bulk import
  })
  .subscribe()

// CORRECT — debounce to absorb bulk operation storms
const debounceRef = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null>(null)

supabase.channel('corporate-changes')
  .on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', table: 'corporate' }, () => {
    if (debounceRef.current) clearTimeout(debounceRef.current)
    debounceRef.current = setTimeout(() => fetchCorporateData(), 2000)
  })
  .subscribe()
```

## Diagnosis Checklist

1. **Check Supabase dashboard** — request type split (database vs API vs storage)
2. **Grep for `refetchInterval`** across the codebase:
   ```bash
   grep -rn "refetchInterval" src/ | sort -t: -k3 -n
   ```
3. **Grep for `setInterval`** in React components:
   ```bash
   grep -rn "setInterval" src/
   ```
4. **Check root-level hooks** (mounted in App.tsx or layout) for missing `staleTime`
5. **Grep for realtime subscriptions** that call full fetches:
   ```bash
   grep -rn "postgres_changes" src/ -A5 | grep -A3 "fetchData\|refetch\|load"
   ```
6. **SSH to VPS** and check for server-side loops:
   ```bash
   ps aux | grep -i <service>; crontab -l; pm2 list
   ```

## Fix Matrix

| Pattern | Fix | Expected Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| `refetchInterval: 5000` on status hook | → `60000` | 12× |
| `refetchInterval: 15000` on approval queries | → `120000` | 8× |
| Root-level count queries without staleTime | Add `staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000` | 5-10× |
| Realtime callback calling full refetch | Debounce 2000ms | Stops cascade |

## Math to Estimate Severity

```
Requests per hour = (60 / interval_seconds) × queries_per_page × concurrent_users × pages_open

Example:
5s interval × 1 query × 5 users × 3 tabs = 180 req/min = 10,800 req/hr = 259,200 req/day
```

## Example Domains

| Domain | Typical Polling Pages | Common Offender |
|---|---|---|
| Hospital management | Bill approvals, OPD queue, pharmacy | Approval status polling at 15s |
| E-commerce admin | Order queue, inventory alerts | Live order count at 5s |
| CRM | Contact sync status, email queue | Sync status polling at 5s |
| SCADA | Tag values, alarm list | Realtime subscription refetch |

## What NOT to Suspect First

- Supabase Edge Functions (would show as API requests, not DB)
- VPS cron jobs (check last — browser is almost always the cause)
- Realtime channel count alone (subscriptions themselves are cheap; it's the callbacks that fetch)

## After Fixing

Deploy and watch Supabase dashboard. Request rate should drop within minutes of the next browser refresh. From 101 req/sec expect drop to under 5 req/sec after fixing intervals and staleTime.

skills.name: Supabase SQL → Clipboard Workflow
skills.description: When `supabase db push` is blocked by historical unapplied migrations on a linked project, copy each new migration's SQL to the macOS clipboard with pbcopy, ask the user to paste into the Supabase SQL editor and Run, then sync the migrations table with `supabase migration repair --status applied <version>`. Never tell the user to open the file and copy by hand.
skills.body:
# Supabase SQL → Clipboard Workflow

## When to use

A `supabase` CLI project linked to production has accumulated old `.sql` files in `supabase/migrations/` that were never applied to the remote DB. Running `supabase db push` produces:

```
Found local migration files to be inserted before the last migration on remote database.
Rerun the command with --include-all flag to apply these migrations:
  supabase/migrations/2025*...
  supabase/migrations/2026*...
```

`--include-all` would apply ALL of those historical migrations against production — usually unsafe (CREATE TABLE without IF NOT EXISTS, schema conflicts with what's actually live, etc.). Instead, ship new migrations one at a time via the Supabase SQL editor and reconcile the migration table by hand.

## The pattern

For every new SQL migration you create in this project:

1. **Copy to clipboard** (do not paraphrase — pipe the file as-is):
   ```bash
   cat supabase/migrations/<file>.sql | pbcopy && \
     echo "Copied $(wc -l < supabase/migrations/<file>.sql | tr -d ' ') lines to clipboard."
   ```

2. **Tell the user**: "SQL is copied to clipboard — paste into the Supabase SQL editor and Run."

   Include the project's SQL-editor URL: `https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<project-ref>/sql/new`

3. **Wait for user confirmation** that the SQL ran successfully.

4. **Sync the migrations table** (run from the project directory, single line — no zsh line breaks):
   ```bash
   cd "/path/to/project" && supabase migration repair --status applied <YYYYMMDDhhmmss>
   ```

## Why this approach

- **`pbcopy`** removes the friction of opening the file and selecting text — one paste, no transcription errors.
- **SQL editor** is idempotent: re-running an `IF NOT EXISTS` migration is harmless if the previous attempt partially failed.
- **`migration repair --status applied`** updates `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` so the file is treated as applied without re-executing — future `db push` runs ignore it.
- **Never `supabase db push --include-all`** unless you've individually verified every pending migration. That flag applies historical migrations in bulk, often catastrophically.

## Pitfalls

- `! supabase ...` works only inside Claude Code's input prompt. In a plain zsh terminal, leading `!` is the logical-NOT operator and short-circuits the rest of the line via `&&`.
- Multi-flag commands like `supabase migration repair --status applied <ver>` must be on a **single line**. zsh splits at line breaks even inside pasted commands.
- `supabase` CLI requires running from the directory that contains `supabase/.temp/project-ref` (or pass `--workdir`). From `~`, it errors with "Cannot find project ref. Have you run supabase link?"
- Write all production-bound migrations as idempotent: `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`, `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS`. For `cron.unschedule`, wrap in `IF EXISTS` guard — `EXCEPTION WHEN undefined_object` is unreliable on newer pg_cron versions which raise `XX000`.

## Example session

```
assistant: Migration is on your clipboard (38 lines). Paste here and Run:
           https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/xvkxccqaopbnkvwgyfjv/sql/new

user:      Success. No rows returned.

assistant: Now sync the migrations table:
           cd "/Users/murali/1backup/Adamrit 11may2026" && \
             supabase migration repair --status applied 20260512000002
```
